distinctions.note: Proprietary means owned by a company with legal rights, and it describes ownership, while closed-source describes whether the code is visible.
Open-source software has public code that anyone can view, change and share, which is the direct opposite of closed-source.

examples.everyday: My phone runs a closed-source operating system, so I can't see how it actually works.
examples.professional: We'll compare the open-source library against the closed-source vendor API before we commit to either one.
examples.analytical: The ethical debate over closed-source AI models turns on whether secrecy about training data and weights can be justified by safety claims.

nuance.analogy: Like a restaurant recipe kept in a locked safe: you can taste the food, but you can't see how it was made.
nuance.etymology: A compound of closed and source, the term arose in computing as the opposite of open source; source comes from Old French sourse, a spring or origin.
common_mistakes: Omitting the hyphen before a noun, as in 'closed source software', which is less standard in American writing.
Using 'closed-source' as a noun, when 'closed source' is the noun form.
Confusing closed-source with proprietary, which refers to legal ownership rather than code visibility.

closed-source.etymology: From *closed* + *source*, in reference to source code.

senses.definition: Causing or undergoing coalescence.
senses.example: The coalescent droplets merged into a single larger drop on the cold glass surface.

senses.definition: Any agent that causes coalescence.
senses.example: In the emulsion, the surfactant acts as a coalescent that helps the oil droplets merge.

core.definition: Coming together and merging into a single mass, group, or form; in genetics, tracing back to a common ancestor.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the third syllable, 'LES'. The middle 'uh' is reduced, so don't say 'co-AL-es-cent' with a full vowel in each syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical; in general writing it can sound pretentious, so 'merging' or 'joining' is often better.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'coalescent' mainly in science, mathematics, statistics, and population genetics, especially in the phrases 'coalescent theory' and 'coalescent model'. In everyday speech, people say 'merging' or 'joining together'. The noun sense, an agent that causes coalescence, is rare and appears mostly in chemistry and materials science.

distinctions.note: Merge is everyday and general; coalescent implies a gradual, natural joining into one body, usually in technical contexts.
Fuse often implies heat, pressure, or a permanent melting together; coalescent is more general and can apply to groups or lineages.
Converge means moving toward a common point; coalesce means actually merging into one unit.

examples.everyday: By the end of the potluck, the two groups' recipes had become so coalescent that everyone just shared one table.
examples.professional: In our phylogenetics pipeline, we use a coalescent model to estimate when two sampled lineages last shared an ancestor.
examples.analytical: Under the coalescent framework, ancestral lineages are traced backward in time until they coalesce into one common ancestor.

nuance.analogy: Like tributaries joining into one river, separate family lines flow backward into a single common source.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'coalescere', to grow together, from 'co-' (together) and 'alescere' (to grow up).
common_mistakes: Confusing 'coalescent' with 'coalition'; 'coalescent' describes things merging into one body, while 'coalition' is a group of allies.
Using 'coalescent' in casual speech where 'merging' sounds more natural.

senses.definition: A male bird, especially:
senses.example: The farmer's cock woke the whole valley before dawn.

senses.definition: A rooster: a male gallinaceous bird, especially a male domestic chicken (Gallus gallus domesticus).
senses.example: Our old cock struts around the coop every morning like he owns the farm.

senses.definition: A cock pigeon.
senses.example: The breeder paired the cock pigeon with a hen from the loft.

senses.definition: A valve or tap for controlling flow in plumbing.
senses.example: The plumber replaced the cock under the kitchen sink that kept dripping.

senses.definition: The hammer of a firearm trigger mechanism.
senses.example: She pulled the cock back slowly before aiming the rifle at the target.

senses.definition: The penis.
senses.example: The anatomy chapter described the cock and testes in clinical detail.

senses.definition: The circle at the end of the rink.
senses.example: The referee waved the player back inside the cock at the end of the rink.

senses.definition: The state of being cocked; an upward turn, tilt or angle.
A boastful tilt of one's head or hat.
senses.example: He gave a cock of his hat and strutted down the street.

senses.definition: A shuttlecock.
senses.example: We spent the afternoon hitting the cock back and forth across the badminton net.

senses.definition: A vane in the shape of a cock; a weathercock.
senses.example: A brass cock on the church steeple spun in the autumn wind.

senses.definition: The crow of a cock, especially the first crow in the morning; cockcrow.
senses.example: We left the camp before the first cock sounded at dawn.

senses.definition: A male fish, especially a salmon or trout.
senses.example: The biologist tagged a cock salmon swimming upstream in the river.

senses.definition: The style or gnomon of a sundial.
senses.example: The cock of the sundial cast a thin shadow across the garden path.

senses.definition: The indicator of a balance.
senses.example: The cock of the scale quivered slightly before settling on zero.

senses.definition: The bridge piece that affords a bearing for the pivot of a balance in a clock or watch.
senses.example: The watchmaker replaced the worn cock that supported the balance wheel pivot.

senses.definition: A small conical pile of hay or grass.
senses.example: The farmhands stack the hay into cocks.

senses.definition: Abbreviation of cock-boat, a type of small boat.
senses.example: We rowed the cock across the harbor to reach the anchored sloop.

senses.definition: (dated) A chief person; a leader or master.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: Vulva, vagina.
To lift the cock of a firearm or crossbow; to prepare (a gun or crossbow) to be fired.
To be prepared to be triggered by having the cock lifted.
senses.example: In the darkness, the gun cocked loudly.

senses.definition: To erect; to turn up.
To turn or twist something upwards or to one side; to lift or tilt (e.g. headwear) boastfully.
senses.example: He cocked his hat jauntily.

senses.definition: To form into piles.
(dated) To turn (the eye) obliquely and partially close its lid, as an expression of derision or insinuation.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: (dated) To strut; to swagger; to look big, pert, or menacing.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: Expression of annoyance.

core.definition: A male chicken; a rooster. In American speech this sense is usually called a rooster.

pronunciation.tip: This is one short syllable with the 'ah' vowel from 'cot' and a hard 'k' at the end. Do not add a 'uh' sound at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in farm or technical contexts, but in casual American speech 'cock' is widely understood as a crude slang term for the male sexual organ, so it can sound vulgar or embarrassing.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English, say 'rooster' for a male chicken, since 'cock' sounds farm-like, old-fashioned, or simply odd. Because of its vulgar slang meaning, avoid 'cock' in casual talk, at work, and in polite company, even when referring to birds. Other senses appear in phrases like 'cock a gun' (to prepare a firearm) and 'cock your head' (to tilt it), which Americans understand without confusion. The interjection 'cock!' expressing annoyance is mainly British.

distinctions.note: 'Rooster' is the normal American word for a male chicken, while 'cock' is more formal, literary, or technical, and it carries a vulgar slang sense.
A hen is a female chicken, the opposite of a cock or rooster, and it has no slang meaning.

examples.everyday: The farm up the road has a rooster that starts crowing at five, so I never sleep in when we visit.
examples.professional: The veterinary report lists the flock as six hens and one cock, with the cock noted for aggression toward new birds.
examples.analytical: Medieval writers used the cock as a symbol of vigilance and, in the Gospels, of Peter's denial.

nuance.analogy: A cock is the bird's male version of a hen, like a bull is to a cow, but in American speech 'rooster' is the everyday word.
nuance.etymology: Old English coc, imitative of the bird's crow.
common_mistakes: Using 'cock' for a rooster in casual American conversation, where it may sound vulgar.
Pronouncing the vowel as a long 'oh' instead of the short 'ah' of 'cot'.
Assuming the phrase 'cock of the roost' is harmless in all settings; it can draw laughter or discomfort.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture the Greek word alektōr (ἀλέκτωρ), meaning rooster, appears in the Gospels. In Mark 14:30 and 14:72, Jesus predicts that Peter will deny him before the cock crows, and Peter's denial follows that sign. Luke 22:34 records the same warning, and the cockcrow becomes a memorable marker of the moment Peter realizes his failure.

cock.etymology: From Middle English *cok*, from Old English *coc*, *cocc* (“cock, male bird”), from **kokk*, from Proto-Germanic **kukkaz* (“cock”), probably of origin.

senses.definition: Overly confident; arrogant and boastful.
Used as a term of endearment, originally for a person of either sex, but later primarily for a man.
senses.example: Morning, cocky, want some coffee before we head out to the fields?

senses.definition: A familiar name for a cockatoo.
senses.example: The farmer's cocky screeched from the gum tree every morning at dawn.

senses.definition: Clipping of cockatoo farmer (“small-scale farmer”); any farmer or owner of rural land.
senses.example: The local cocky sold his wheat at the regional market after a dry season.

core.definition: Overly confident in a way that seems arrogant or boastful.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, KAH. The second syllable is a clear, light ee, not a long oh or a reduced uh.

nuance.connotation: Negative: it suggests arrogance, though it can be playful when describing a kid or an athlete.
nuance.usage_note: This is common informal American English for someone who is overly confident or boastful. It can be affectionate for a kid or a sports fan and critical for a coworker. The noun senses (a term of endearment, cockatoo, or a farmer) are regional or Australian, so avoid them in American conversation.

distinctions.note: Confident is positive and based on ability; cocky is negative or playful and suggests the confidence goes too far.
Arrogant is stronger and more serious, implying contempt for others; cocky is lighter and more informal.

examples.everyday: Don't get too cocky just because you won one game; the season isn't over yet.
examples.professional: The new hire was cocky in the meeting, but his analysis held up, so the team respected him in the end.
examples.analytical: Cockiness in argument often works as a rhetorical shield, substituting a confident tone for evidence.

nuance.analogy: Like a rooster on a fence post, crowing as if the whole farm belongs to it.
nuance.etymology: From cock (rooster) plus -y, used since the 1800s of strutting, boastful behavior.
common_mistakes: Confusing cocky with cockeyed, which means crooked or absurd.
Pronouncing the second syllable with a long oh sound.

senses.definition: A short textual designation, often with little relation to the item it represents.
senses.example: This flavor of soup has been assigned the code WRT-9.

senses.definition: A body of law, sanctioned by legislation, in which the rules of law to be specifically applied by the courts are set forth in systematic form; a compilation of laws by public authority; a digest.
senses.example: The state's code of civil procedure sets out the rules courts must follow in lawsuits.

senses.definition: Any system of principles, rules or regulations relating to one subject.
senses.example: The medical code is a system of rules for the regulation of the professional conduct of physicians.

senses.definition: A set of rules for converting information into another form or representation.
senses.example: The ASCII code of "A" is 65.

senses.definition: (by synecdoche) A codeword, code point, an encoded representation of a character, symbol, or other entity.
senses.example: The ASCII code of "A" is 65.

senses.definition: A message represented by rules intended to conceal its meaning.
senses.example: The spies sent messages in code so that enemy agents could not read them.

senses.definition: A cryptographic system using a codebook that converts words or phrases into codewords.
senses.example: The diplomats used a code book to turn each name into a short numeric code word.

senses.definition: Instructions for a computer, written in a programming language; the input of a translator, an interpreter or a browser, namely: source code, machine code, bytecode.
senses.example: Object-oriented C++ code is easier to understand for a human than C code.

senses.definition: A program.
senses.example: I wrote a short code that automatically renames every photo in my folder by date.

senses.definition: A particular lect or language variety.
senses.example: Her grandmother spoke a regional code that few outsiders could follow.

senses.definition: A set of unwritten rules that bind a social group.
senses.example: girl code

senses.definition: An emergency requiring situation-trained members of the staff.
senses.example: When the nurse called a code on the ward, three staff members rushed to the room.

senses.definition: To write software programs.
senses.example: I learned to code on an early home computer in the 1980s.

senses.definition: To add codes to (a data set).
senses.example: Before training the model, we code the survey responses into categories by hand.

senses.definition: To categorize by assigning identifiers from a schedule, for example CPT coding for medical insurance purposes.
senses.example: The billing office must code each procedure correctly so the insurer will pay the claim.

senses.definition: To encode.
senses.example: We should code the messages we send out on Usenet.

senses.definition: To encode a protein.
senses.example: Each gene is transcribed and translated to code for a specific protein in the cell.

senses.definition: To call a hospital emergency code.
senses.example: coding in the CT scanner

senses.definition: Of a patient, to suffer a sudden medical emergency (a code blue) such as cardiac arrest.
senses.example: During the night shift, the elderly patient began to code and needed immediate CPR.

core.definition: A system of letters, numbers or symbols used to represent something, such as a zip code, area code or promo code.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is a diphthong that glides from 'oh' toward 'oo', and the final d is voiced and clearly pronounced. Do not shorten it to 'cod', and do not add a vowel after the d.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use code constantly in everyday life for zip codes, area codes, promo codes and dress codes. In professional settings, it often means computer programs or the written text of software. The legal sense, a systematic collection of laws, appears in phrases like the tax code. The verb to code, meaning to write software, is very common in tech.

distinctions.note: A cipher transforms text letter by letter using a method, while a code replaces words or phrases with agreed symbols, although many people use the two words loosely.
A password is a secret used to gain access, while a code can be any system of symbols, including public ones like zip codes.

examples.everyday: Can you send me the promo code again? I lost the email.
examples.professional: I pushed the fix to the branch, so please review the code before Friday's release.
examples.analytical: A code, in this sense, is a convention that fixes the meaning of each symbol for everyone who uses the system.

nuance.analogy: A code is like a nickname: short, agreed on by a group, and useful only when everyone knows what it stands for.
nuance.etymology: From Latin codex, meaning a block of wood or a book, through Old French code.
common_mistakes: Saying 'write a code' for software; in tech, code is usually uncountable, so say 'write code' or 'a piece of code'.
Pronouncing it like 'cod' with a short vowel.

code.etymology: From Middle English *code* (“system of law”), from Old French *code* (“system of law”), from Latin *cōdex*, later form of *caudex* (“the stock or stem of a tree, a board or tablet of wood smeared over with wax, on which the ancients originally wrote;…

senses.definition: The state of two or more things existing together, usually in a temporal or spatial sense, with or without mutual interaction.
senses.example: Many cities show peaceful coexistence between old churches and modern glass towers.

core.definition: The state of two or more things existing together at the same time or in the same place.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on ZIS, and the final -ence is a reduced, unstressed syllable that sounds like 'uns'. Do not give the ending a full 'ens' vowel, and keep the t clear.

nuance.connotation: Positive in political and social contexts, where peaceful coexistence is valued; neutral in science, where it simply describes overlap.
nuance.usage_note: Peaceful coexistence is a standard American phrase in news, politics and history, such as discussions of different faiths or neighboring countries. In casual talk, people more often say we get along or we manage to live together. The word is perfectly ordinary but sounds slightly formal in a casual chat.

distinctions.note: Cohabitation means living together as a couple in one home, often unmarried; coexistence is broader and need not involve sharing a home or any relationship.
Harmony implies agreement, cooperation or pleasant balance, while coexistence says only that two things persist side by side, even with tension.

examples.everyday: My neighbors and I have a pretty good coexistence: they keep their dog off my lawn, and I keep my music down after ten.
examples.professional: The product team and the platform team reached an agreement on shared deployment windows, which made coexistence much easier.
examples.analytical: Peaceful coexistence between religious communities has historically depended on political arrangements that protected minorities.

nuance.analogy: Like two families sharing a long hallway, each with their own door, each respecting the other's space.
nuance.etymology: From co- (together) plus existence, from Latin existere, to come forth or stand forth.
common_mistakes: Stressing the final syllable, -ence, instead of ZIS.
Pronouncing the final -ence with a full vowel instead of a reduced sound.
Using coexistence to mean friendship; it implies two things persisting, not affection.

senses.definition: Designed to be collapsed, especially so as to be more compact when not in use.
senses.example: collapsible shovel

senses.definition: Any object that can be collapsed to save space.
A kind of boat that can be collapsed for greater portability.
A display element that can be collapsed to hide it from view.

core.definition: Designed to fold or compress flat so that it takes up less space when not in use.

pronunciation.tip: Stress LAPS, the second syllable, and make the -ible ending sound like -uh-bul, not -eeble. The middle syllable is a quick schwa.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It describes a practical feature that makes objects easier to store or carry.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use collapsible for items such as strollers, chairs, tents, water bottles, and containers, and it is common in product descriptions. For phones or screens that fold, foldable is also common. The noun sense, meaning an object that collapses, is rare; say collapsible item or the specific product name.

distinctions.note: Foldable suggests bending along a line, while collapsible suggests a structure that compresses or telescopes into a smaller size.
Portable means easy to carry; collapsible means it can also be made smaller for storage, though it may not be light.

examples.everyday: We bought a collapsible stroller, so it fits in the trunk when we go to the zoo.
examples.professional: The trade show team needs collapsible display stands that can be packed into two cases for shipping.
examples.analytical: The designer argued that a collapsible structure reflects a broader cultural preference for flexibility over permanence.

nuance.analogy: A collapsible chair is like a telescope: it shrinks down to a compact form without losing its essential shape.
nuance.etymology: From collapse, from Latin collapsus, fallen together, plus the suffix -ible, meaning able to be.
common_mistakes: Misspelling it as collapsable, which is a common error even though collapsible is standard.
Using collapsible for a product that merely folds flat, where foldable is more natural.

senses.definition: A battle, a fight (often one in which weapons are used).
senses.example: The soldiers returned from combat with stories they rarely shared with their families.

senses.definition: A struggle for victory.
To fight; to struggle against.
senses.example: It has proven very difficult to combat drug addiction.

senses.definition: To fight (with); to struggle for victory (against).
senses.example: Doctors in the clinic combat misinformation by sharing clear, accurate facts with patients.

core.definition: Fighting, especially armed fighting between opposing forces, or a determined struggle against something harmful.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and keep the second as a lighter 'bat' with a clear b and the short a of 'cat'. Don't put the main stress on the end.

nuance.connotation: Negative or serious; it implies violence, conflict or a hard struggle.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use combat most often for armed fighting in war, as in combat troops or combat boots, and in sports for serious contests such as combat sports. In everyday speech, combat against something is a more general struggle, like combating climate change or fighting poverty. For casual disputes or friendly contests, fight, argument or match is more natural.

distinctions.note: Battle names a specific engagement or a long conflict, while combat is a broader term for fighting in general, especially physical or armed.
Fight is the most everyday word and can mean a quarrel or a brawl, while combat sounds more serious, organized or military.

examples.everyday: Those guys saw combat in Vietnam, and my grandfather never talks much about it, even when we ask.
examples.professional: Our security team engages in daily combat against phishing emails, and new attacks arrive every hour.
examples.analytical: Augustine described the inner combat of the will as a struggle as real as any battle fought between nations.

nuance.analogy: Combat is like a tug-of-war between two forces, where one side must gain ground for the other to lose it.
nuance.etymology: From French combattre, from Latin combattere, to fight together.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in 'kom-BAT'
Using combat for a friendly argument or a sports match, where fight or match is more natural

combat.etymology: 16th century, Middle French *combat*, deverbal from Old French *combatre*, from Vulgar Latin **combattere*, from Latin *com-* (“with”) + *battuere* (“to beat, strike”).

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to the combination and arrangement of elements in sets.
Of, pertaining to, or involving combinations.
senses.example: The combinatorial explosion of possible test cases made exhaustive testing impossible.

core.definition: Relating to counting or arranging the possible combinations of elements in a set.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TOR, with a secondary stress on KAHM. Say the r clearly before the ee sound, and end with a light 'ul'. Don't stress the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and specialized. It is a precise term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use combinatorial mainly in mathematics, computer science and data science, as in combinatorial problem or combinatorial optimization. Outside technical settings it sounds unusual. Don't confuse it with combinational, which describes logic circuits.

distinctions.note: Combinational describes logic circuits whose outputs depend only on current inputs; combinatorial describes counting or arranging sets.
Combined is general and everyday, meaning merged; combinatorial is a technical term for counting arrangements.

examples.everyday: My sister does combinatorial puzzles for fun, like counting all the ways to arrange the tiles.
examples.professional: The scheduler is hard because it solves a combinatorial optimization problem with thousands of constraints.
examples.analytical: A combinatorial argument proves the identity by counting the same set of objects in two different ways.

nuance.analogy: Like counting every outfit you can build from a pile of shirts and pants.
nuance.etymology: From combination plus -al, ultimately from Latin combinare 'to join together'.
common_mistakes: Confusing combinatorial with combinational, which refers to logic circuits.
Stressing the first syllable instead of the strong TOR syllable.

senses.definition: To honor the memory of someone or something with a ceremony or object.
senses.example: On November 11th we commemorate the fallen with a march.

senses.definition: To serve as a memorial to someone or something.
senses.example: The cenotaph commemorates the fallen.

core.definition: Honoring the memory of a person, event, or achievement through a ceremony, holiday, monument, or similar observance.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the MEM syllable, and the middle syllables are reduced to a schwa, so avoid saying 'commem-er-ating'. The ending '-ating' is pronounced 'ay-ting' with a short, unstressed 'ing'.

nuance.connotation: Positive
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'commemorating' for holidays, anniversaries, and public ceremonies, such as a plaque commemorating a historic event. In casual speech, people say 'celebrating' for happy occasions or 'remembering' for losses. The word sounds formal, so it fits announcements, programs, and speeches better than a casual chat.

distinctions.note: Celebrating emphasizes joy and festivity, while commemorating focuses on honoring and remembering a person or event.
Memorializing usually refers to creating a memorial, and commemorating can also mean holding an event without a permanent monument.

examples.everyday: We're having a barbecue Saturday, commemorating Grandpa's eightieth birthday.
examples.professional: The team is commemorating our tenth product launch with a short video and a lunch on Friday.
examples.analytical: The monument, commemorating the dead, forces visitors to confront how a nation chooses what to remember.

nuance.analogy: Like a bookmark in history, which marks a page so people will return to it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin commemorare, 'to call to mind together', from com- plus memor, 'mindful'.
common_mistakes: Using 'commemorate' for ordinary remembering; say 'remember' in everyday talk.
Pronouncing the middle syllables with a strong /ɚ/ rather than a weak schwa.
nuance.biblical_note: In Hebrew the idea is zikkaron, 'remembrance' or 'memorial', which is used for the Passover in Exodus 12:14 (RSV: 'a memorial day'), where Israel is told to keep the day as a remembrance of the Lord's deliverance from Egypt. In the New Testament, Jesus says at the Last Supper, 'Do this in remembrance of me' (Luke 22:19 RSV), and Paul repeats the command in 1 Corinthians 11:24-25 RSV, linking the meal to remembering Christ's death. These passages show that commemoration in Scripture is an act of remembering God's saving acts, not only a civic observance.

senses.definition: A sending or mission (to do or accomplish something).
senses.example: The church sent her on a commission to rebuild schools in the drought-stricken valley.

senses.definition: An official charge or authority to do something, often used of military officers.
senses.example: David received his commission after graduating from West Point.

senses.definition: The thing to be done as agent for another.
senses.example: I have three commissions for the city.

senses.definition: A body or group of people, officially tasked with carrying out a particular function.
senses.example: the European Commission

senses.definition: A fee charged by an agent or broker for carrying out a transaction.
senses.example: a reseller's commission

senses.definition: A bonus in pay awarded to a salesperson for selling a particular, secretly sponsored product, for which the sponsor will reimburse the employer.
senses.example: He earned a commission on every energy drink he sold, though customers never knew who sponsored it.

senses.definition: A payment by a fan to an artist, after which the artist will produce a work of art requested by the fan.
senses.example: She paid a commission to an illustrator for a portrait of her late dog.

senses.definition: The act of committing (e.g. a crime or error).
senses.example: the commission, preparation or instigation of an act of terrorism

senses.definition: To send or officially charge someone or some group to do something.
senses.example: James Bond was commissioned with recovering the secret documents.

senses.definition: To place an order for (often a piece of art).
senses.example: He commissioned a replica of the Mona Lisa for his living room, but the painter gave up after six months.

senses.definition: To put (a ship or boat, etc.) into active service.
senses.example: The aircraft carrier was commissioned in 1944, during WWII.

core.definition: A payment, usually a percentage of a sale, given to someone who sells something for you or on your behalf.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MISH, the second syllable. The -sion ending is pronounced 'shun', not 'zhun', and the final vowel is reduced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a fair payment for work, though people may view high commissions with suspicion, especially when the seller benefits more than the buyer.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'commission' often in sales, real estate, insurance and finance. People say they work 'on commission' or 'for commission', meaning their pay depends on sales. Commission also means an official appointment or an order for art, so context matters.

distinctions.note: A salary is a fixed amount paid regularly, while a commission varies with the amount of business you bring in.
A fee is a set charge for a service, while a commission is a percentage of the value of a transaction.
A bonus is an extra payment for good performance, while a commission is built into the pay structure for each sale.

examples.everyday: I'm paid partly in commission, so slow months really hurt.
examples.professional: The new commission structure rewards reps who close multi-year contracts instead of short renewals.
examples.analytical: A commission divides the seller's reward from the product's value, which can shape the advice the seller gives the buyer.

nuance.analogy: A commission is like a tip paid to a server, but calculated as a percentage of each sale and paid by the business rather than the customer.
nuance.etymology: From Latin commissio, from committere meaning to entrust, bring together or put in charge.
common_mistakes: Saying 'a commission of 5% from each sale' instead of 'a 5% commission on each sale'.
Confusing commission (payment for sales) with commissary (a store or food supply on a base or in a company).

commission.etymology: From Middle English *commissioun*, from Old French *commission*, from Latin *commissiō* (“sending together; commission”), from *committō* + *-tiō*, from *com-* (“with”) + *mittō* (“to send”).

senses.definition: That which is known by most people, and thus cannot reasonably be contested.
senses.example: That the Earth orbits the sun is common knowledge, so nobody in my class questioned it.

senses.definition: A special kind of knowledge for a group of agents, such that when all the agents in a group G know p, they all know that they know p, they all know that they all know that they know p, and so on ad infinitum.
senses.example: In the puzzle, every agent knows the rule, and it is common knowledge among all players.

core.definition: Information that most people know and accept as true, so it does not need to be explained or proven.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on NAH in knowledge, and the final -dge is pronounced like a soft j. The silent k in know is often forgotten, and the second syllable of knowledge is a reduced schwa.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can sound helpful when reminding people of something obvious, but condescending if used to imply someone should already know it.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'It's common knowledge that...' in everyday talk to present something as widely known. Saying it to someone who did not know can sound slightly patronizing, so soften it with 'I assumed everyone knew...'. A natural reply is 'Oh, I didn't know that.'

distinctions.note: General knowledge is broad facts across many subjects, as in a trivia game; common knowledge is what most people in a given community know.
Public knowledge refers to information officially released or publicly available; common knowledge is what people already assume is widely known.

examples.everyday: It's common knowledge that the best bagels in this city come from that little place on Fifth.
examples.professional: It's common knowledge on the team that the pipeline breaks every Friday, so we should add monitoring.
examples.analytical: In game theory, common knowledge requires that everyone knows p, knows that everyone knows p, and so on without end.

nuance.analogy: Like a sign everyone in town has already read, so nobody needs to point it out.
nuance.etymology: Common comes from Latin communis; knowledge comes from Middle English knowleche, from know.
common_mistakes: Using 'common knowledge' for facts that are only known to a small group, which sounds incorrect to American ears.
Mispronouncing the -ledge ending as 'ledj' with a full vowel instead of a soft 'lij'.

senses.definition: One who composes; an author.
senses.example: She was the composer of a bestselling history of the Roman empire.

senses.definition: Especially, one who composes music.
senses.example: The composer spent years writing a symphony for the orchestra.

senses.definition: One who, or that which, quiets or calms.
senses.example: Lavender oil acts as a composer for frayed nerves after a long day.

core.definition: A person who writes music, such as symphonies, songs, or film scores.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on POH, the second syllable. The final -er is a clear American r, so say 'zer' with the r sound, not 'zuh' or 'zoh'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It names a respected creative professional.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English, composer almost always means a music writer. For someone who writes books or articles, Americans say writer or author; composer in that sense sounds literary or old-fashioned. Many people say songwriter for popular music, while composer is more common for classical, film, or game music.

distinctions.note: A songwriter usually writes lyrics and melody for popular songs, while a composer often writes instrumental or orchestral music, scores, or longer works.
An arranger adapts existing music for different instruments or voices; a composer creates new music from scratch.

examples.everyday: My cousin is a composer who writes music for TV commercials.
examples.professional: We need a composer to write the theme music for the app's launch video by Friday.
examples.analytical: The composer's late quartets reject the tonal logic that his earlier symphonies depended on.

nuance.analogy: A composer is like an architect of sound: they draw the blueprint, the score, and musicians build it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin componere, 'to put together', through the verb compose.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, saying 'KUM-po-zer' instead of 'kum-POH-zer'.
Dropping the r at the end, which sounds British to many Americans.

senses.definition: Having factors other than itself and one; not prime and not one.
Made up of multiple components; compound or complex.
senses.example: The building's composite structure combines a steel frame with reinforced concrete floors.

senses.definition: Belonging to the Asteraceae family (formerly known as Compositae), bearing involucrate heads of many small florets.
senses.example: The sunflower is a composite plant whose flower heads contain hundreds of tiny florets.

senses.definition: Being a mixture of Ionic and Corinthian styles.
senses.example: The arch on the facade is composite, blending Ionic volutes with Corinthian acanthus leaves.

senses.definition: (historical) Employing multiple exposures on a single plate, so as to create an average view of something, such as faces in physiognomy.
senses.example: composite portraiture; a composite photograph
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: A function of a function.
senses.example: The composite of two functions is itself a function, so we can differentiate it using the chain rule.

senses.definition: A mixture of different components.
senses.example: The paint is a composite of resin, pigment, and crushed glass.

senses.definition: A structural material that gains its strength from a combination of complementary materials.
senses.example: The bicycle frame uses a carbon fiber composite that is lighter than aluminum.

senses.definition: Clipping of composite number.
senses.example: Is 91 a composite? Yes, because it equals seven times thirteen.

senses.definition: A framed photo board composed of many individual photos of fraternity or sorority members.
senses.example: Every fraternity brother's photo appears on the composite hanging in the lobby.

senses.definition: The separate pages of individual student photos that form the main section.
senses.example: Her senior composite includes a small portrait and a short quote from every student.

senses.definition: A plant belonging to the family Asteraceae, syn. Compositae.
senses.example: Dandelions and daisies are both composite plants found across most of the country.

senses.definition: A drawing, photograph, etc. that combines several separate pictures or images.
senses.example: The detective pinned a composite of the suspect's face, built from several witness descriptions, to the wall.

senses.definition: (uncommon) A segment, subset.
senses.example: The final composite of the project covers only the results from the last quarter.
senses.label: uncommon

senses.definition: To make a composite.
senses.example: I composited an image using computer software.

core.definition: Having factors other than one and itself, so it is not prime. Applies to whole numbers greater than one, such as 9 or 12.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, and pronounce the 'o' as the short 'ah' of American 'hot.' The final syllable is reduced to 'it,' so don't say 'composite' with a long 'ite' ending.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise mathematical classification with no evaluative meaning.
nuance.usage_note: In math classes, Americans say 'composite number' when contrasting it with 'prime number.' Outside math, 'composite' also means 'made of several parts,' as in 'composite material' or 'composite photo.' Use the math sense only when talking about numbers.

distinctions.note: Prime numbers have only two factors, one and themselves. Composite numbers have more factors, and the two words are opposites in math.
Compound means made of two or more parts combined, and is common in chemistry and grammar. Composite in math is a strict property of whole numbers.

examples.everyday: That photo is a composite of three different shots, so the lighting looks perfect.
examples.professional: Our customer churn metric is a composite score built from usage, billing and support data.
examples.analytical: Because 91 equals 7 times 13, it is composite rather than prime.

nuance.analogy: A composite number is like a Lego model built from smaller bricks, while a prime is a single brick.
nuance.etymology: From Latin compositus, 'put together,' the past participle of componere.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'composite number' with 'complex number,' which is a different concept.
Pronouncing the middle vowel as a long 'o,' as in 'kom-POZ-ite.'

composite.etymology: Borrowed from Middle French *composite*, from Latin *compositus*, past participle of *compōnō* (“put together”).

senses.definition: Able to be compressed.

Of a surface embedded in a 3-dimensional manifold, containing a circle that does not serve as the boundary of a disk that lies in the surface, but does serve as boundary of a disk that lies in the ambient manifold.

core.definition: Able to be pressed into a smaller volume when force is applied.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, and the final -ible is a weak 'uh-bul', not 'eye-bul'. Keep the middle syllables short and unstressed.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a descriptive word with no emotional weight.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'compressible' in science and everyday talk about objects that can be squished flat, such as boxes, foam, and gases. Something that cannot be compressed is 'incompressible', and that word is common in engineering and fluid mechanics. In casual speech, people more often say something 'squishes' or 'squashes down' than use this word.

distinctions.note: Compressible describes the ability to be squeezed, while compressed describes the state of having been squeezed already.
Squishy is informal and describes a soft texture, while compressible is a precise term for a material's ability to be reduced in volume.

examples.everyday: Don't worry, the box is compressible, so you can squash it flat before you put it in the recycling.
examples.professional: Our foam gasket is compressible enough to seal the lid, but it springs back after the door opens.
examples.analytical: A gas is highly compressible, so its volume changes sharply when pressure rises, unlike a liquid, which barely changes at all.

nuance.analogy: Like a pillow: you can press it down, and it becomes smaller until you let go.
nuance.etymology: From Latin comprimere, 'to press together', through the verb compress and the suffix -ible.
common_mistakes: Saying 'compressable' with an a, which is a common misspelling.
Pronouncing the ending as 'eye-bul' instead of 'uh-bul'.

senses.definition: Capable of being computed, or enumerated.
senses.example: The total number of possible outcomes is computable, so we can enumerate every case before running the simulation.

senses.definition: Of a problem, solvable by a Turing machine or any thereto Turing-equivalent model; Turing-computable.
senses.example: Logicians proved that the halting problem is not computable, so no program can decide it for every input.

senses.definition: Of a number, able to be approximated to arbitrary precision by a computable function.
senses.example: Pi is a computable number, since algorithms can approximate it to any desired precision.

senses.definition: Of a countably infinite set, having a computable indicator function.
senses.example: A computable set of integers has an indicator function that a program can evaluate for any given integer.

core.definition: Able to be calculated or solved by a systematic procedure, such as an algorithm or a Turing machine.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on PYOO, and the final -able reduces to a quiet 'uh-buhl'. The middle t is a flap in American speech, so it sounds almost like a quick d.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term in logic and mathematics, and it carries no positive or negative feeling.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use computable almost only in logic, computer science and math courses, and in talks about what machines can or cannot solve. In everyday conversation you would say 'can be calculated' or 'can be worked out'. Saying 'this problem is computable' in a meeting signals that you mean it can be solved in principle by an algorithm, not that it is quick or practical.

distinctions.note: Computable means that a result can be obtained by some algorithm in principle, while computational describes the process or methods of computing, as in computational biology.

Calculable is the everyday word for something that can be worked out with numbers, while computable is the stricter term that implies a formal procedure and is used in logic and theory of computation.

examples.everyday: Honestly, I don't think a question like that is even computable; people just guess.
examples.professional: Before we commit to the project, we need to confirm that the optimization problem is computable within our time budget.
examples.analytical: Gödel's argument shows that not every truth about arithmetic is computable by a fixed formal system.

nuance.analogy: Like a recipe that a machine can follow step by step to the end, a computable problem is one where some finite set of instructions always reaches an answer.
nuance.etymology: From 'compute' plus the suffix -able; 'compute' comes from Latin computare, 'to reckon together'.
common_mistakes: Using computable for everyday numbers to mean 'easy to count', when calculable or countable is more natural.
Mispronouncing the stress as KOM-pyoo-tuh-buhl instead of kum-PYOO-tuh-buhl.

senses.definition: The act, process or ability of concentrating; the process of becoming concentrated, or the state of being concentrated.
senses.example: Her concentration during the exam was so intense that she didn't notice the fire alarm.

senses.definition: The direction of attention to a specific object.
senses.example: His concentration on the chess board never wavered during the three-hour match.

senses.definition: The act, process or product of reducing the volume of a liquid, as by evaporation.
senses.example: The chef used a long simmer for the concentration of the tomato sauce.

senses.definition: The act or process of removing the dress of ore and of reducing the valuable part to smaller compass, as by currents of air or water.
senses.example: The mill used water currents for the concentration of the copper ore.

senses.definition: A field or course of study on which one focuses, especially as a student in a college or university.
senses.example: She chose statistics as her concentration because she loved working with data.

senses.definition: The proportion of a substance in a whole.
senses.example: The sample showed a high concentration of lead in the old paint.

senses.definition: The matching game pelmanism.
senses.example: We played concentration with the kids, flipping cards to find matching pairs.

senses.definition: The amount of solute in a solution measured in suitable units (e.g. parts per million (ppm))
senses.example: The lab report lists the concentration of nitrate as 12 parts per million.

core.definition: The ability to focus your attention on one thing for a sustained period without getting distracted.

pronunciation.tip: Main stress falls on TRAY, with a light secondary stress on KAHN. The -tion ending is pronounced 'shun,' and the middle syllable is weak, so don't say each vowel fully.

nuance.connotation: Positive. Good concentration is valued in school, work and sports, though losing it is simply a neutral fact of life.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use concentration in everyday talk about focus, as in 'I need more concentration on this.' Casual speakers more often say 'focus.' In statistics and economics, concentration describes how a total is spread out, such as market concentration or a concentration index. In chemistry, it means the amount of a substance dissolved in a solution.

distinctions.note: Focus is the everyday word for directing attention. Concentration is slightly more formal and emphasizes sustained effort.
Attention is the general ability to notice. Concentration is intense, sustained attention on one task.

examples.everyday: I lost my concentration when the kids started yelling in the next room.
examples.professional: Our concentration risk is high: three clients account for almost half of our revenue.
examples.analytical: Her argument depends on the concentration of attention: without sustained focus, the reasoning falls apart before the conclusion.

nuance.analogy: Like a lens that bends scattered sunlight to one sharp point, concentration gathers your scattered thoughts onto one task.
nuance.etymology: From concentrate, from Latin concentrare, to bring to a single center, with the suffix -ion.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle syllable with a full vowel (KAHN-sen-TRAY-shun) instead of a weak sun
Using concentration with 'to' instead of 'on' (concentration on the task, not concentration to the task)

concentration.etymology: From New Latin *concentrātiō* (“(1550) action or an act of coming together at a single place; (1659) extraction or separation of one or more of the metals present in an alloy”).

senses.definition: In a conclusive manner; with finality; decisively.
senses.example: Once the final experiment had been performed, the theory was conclusively proved.

senses.definition: By way of conclusion.
senses.example: The forensic team conclusively linked the fingerprints to the suspect, ending the investigation.

core.definition: In a way that settles a question beyond doubt; decisively.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, KLOO, and keep the first syllable light. The -ive is short, and the final -ly is a clear 'lee' with a reduced middle vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It signals certainty and finality about evidence or results.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use conclusively when a test, study, or piece of evidence ends a debate: 'The DNA test conclusively proved his innocence.' It is common in news and science writing but sounds formal in casual talk, where people say 'for sure' or 'definitely.' Do not use it to open your closing remarks in speech; say 'in conclusion' or 'to sum up' instead.

distinctions.note: Definitively emphasizes that a matter is settled for good, while conclusively emphasizes that the evidence leaves no doubt.
Decisively describes firm, quick action or a clear win, while conclusively is mainly used for proof and evidence.

examples.everyday: The mechanic checked the wheels and ruled out the brakes conclusively, so the noise must be the belt.
examples.professional: Our A/B test conclusively showed that the new checkout flow increased conversions by four percent.
examples.analytical: Hume argued that no amount of past experience can conclusively establish a necessary connection between cause and effect.

nuance.analogy: Conclusively is like a judge's gavel: the case is closed and no one can reopen it.
nuance.etymology: From conclusive, from Medieval Latin conclusivus, 'closing', plus the adverbial suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Starting a spoken conclusion with 'Conclusively,' which sounds odd; say 'In conclusion' or 'To sum up' instead.
Pronouncing the second syllable with a long i, as in kun-KLOO-syve-lee; the vowel is short, as in kun-KLOO-siv-lee.

senses.definition: Of, pertaining to, or being a confederation.
senses.example: The confederal government had little power to tax, so the states funded most projects.

core.definition: Relating to a confederation, a loose union of states in which the member governments keep most of the power.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, -FED-, not the first. The middle syllable is a reduced, r-colored vowel, and the word ends in a soft 'ul'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical, used in political science and history.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mostly in political science, law and history, such as discussions of the Articles of Confederation, which created a confederal system. Ordinary speakers would say 'loose alliance' or 'league of states'. Be careful with 'Confederate', which in the US usually refers to the Confederate States during the Civil War.

distinctions.note: Federal describes a system where the central government holds substantial authority over the states, while confederal describes one where the states hold most of the power.
Confederate, capitalized, usually means the Confederate States of America in US history, so it is a sensitive word outside that context.

examples.everyday: Our book club argued all night about whether a confederal setup could really hold together.
examples.professional: The partner companies proposed a confederal governance model, with each unit keeping its own budget and veto.
examples.analytical: A confederal constitution leaves sovereignty with the member states, so the central body depends on their continued consent.

nuance.analogy: Like a neighborhood association in which each block keeps its own rules and only a few decisions are shared.
nuance.etymology: From confederate, from Latin confoederare 'to unite by a treaty,' from foedus 'league, treaty'.
common_mistakes: Confusing confederal with federal, which describes a much stronger central government.
Stressing the first syllable as KON-fed-ral, which is a common error for Americans to notice.

senses.definition: The property of being confidential.
senses.example: The doctor reminded the nurses that patient confidentiality is required by federal law.

senses.definition: Something told in confidence; a secret.
senses.example: He whispered a confidentiality about the layoffs, trusting me to keep it between us.

core.definition: The quality or state of being kept private and not shared with people who are not authorized to know it.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on the al syllable, so say shee-AL-uh-tee. Stress shifts from confidential to confidentiality, so do not keep the stress on DEN. The -tial becomes shee, and the final -ty is a short tee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It describes a protection that builds trust, especially in medicine, law, and business.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use confidentiality in legal, medical, and workplace contexts, as in 'Patient confidentiality is protected by law.' It sounds formal, so in casual conversation people usually say keep it private or keep it between us. A common professional phrase is signing a confidentiality agreement or NDA.

distinctions.note: Privacy is the broader right to be left alone or to control personal information, while confidentiality is the duty to keep specific information secret.
Secrecy often implies hiding something, sometimes deliberately from the public, while confidentiality is a protection of information shared under trust.

examples.everyday: The clinic guaranteed confidentiality, so I felt comfortable sharing my medical history.
examples.professional: Please sign the confidentiality agreement before you get access to the customer database.
examples.analytical: Confidentiality is not merely a legal duty but a condition under which trust, and therefore honest disclosure, becomes possible.

nuance.analogy: Confidentiality is like a lock on a diary; it only works if everyone who has a key agrees not to use it.
nuance.etymology: From confidential plus the noun suffix -ity, from Latin confidere, to trust.
common_mistakes: Using confidentiality as a countable noun; say the confidentiality of the records, not a confidentiality.
Keeping the stress on the DEN syllable, as in kon-fi-DEN-shee-al-i-tee.

senses.definition: The act of congratulating.
senses.example: a short speech of congratulation

core.definition: An expression of happiness about someone's success or good news, usually heard in the plural form 'congratulations.'

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LAY, and the final syllable is a reduced 'shun.' The 'tu' is pronounced 'ch,' so the middle sounds like 'GRATCH-uh.'

nuance.connotation: Positive. It expresses warm support and happiness for someone else.
nuance.usage_note: Americans almost always say the plural 'congratulations' as a set phrase, as in 'Congratulations on your new job!' The singular noun is more formal, used for a formal note or speech. A natural reply to 'congratulations' is 'Thank you so much.'

distinctions.note: 'Congratulations' is the everyday plural form used in speech and cards, while the singular 'congratulation' sounds more formal or stiff.
'Praise' is an expression of approval for quality or effort, while 'congratulation' focuses on being happy about a specific success.

examples.everyday: Congratulations on the new house! You must be so excited to move in.
examples.professional: A quick congratulation to Maria for closing the deal, that was excellent work.
examples.analytical: The congratulation given to a high achiever can quietly reveal what a community values most.

nuance.analogy: A congratulation is like a small flag planted on someone's success, so everyone can see that you are glad for them.
nuance.etymology: From Latin congratulatio, from congratulari, meaning 'to rejoice together.'
common_mistakes: Using the singular 'a congratulation' in casual talk, where 'congratulations' is standard.
Pronouncing the middle as 'GRAT-yoo-LAY-shun' instead of 'grach-uh-LAY-shun.'

congratulation.etymology: From Middle English *congratulacion*, from Middle French *congratulation* or its etymon Latin *congratulatio*, from *congrātulor* (“to congratulate”).

senses.definition: Any of the four distinct shapes that are the intersections of a cone with a plane, namely the circle, ellipse, parabola, and hyperbola.

core.definition: Any of the curves (circle, ellipse, parabola, or hyperbola) formed when a flat plane slices through a cone.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second word, SEK, with a short e. 'Conic' sounds like 'tonic' and must not be pronounced as 'cone-ik,' which confuses it with the solid 'cone.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise mathematical term used in classrooms and technical work.
nuance.usage_note: American high schools and colleges teach conic sections in precalculus, analytic geometry, and calculus courses. Outside math, Americans rarely use the term, so in casual speech a student might say 'the parabola or the circle' instead. The phrase is usually plural in discussion, as in 'the conic sections.'

distinctions.note: Conical means shaped like a cone. Conic is the technical adjective for curves produced by cutting a cone, as in conic section.
Every conic section can be described by a second-degree equation in two variables, but quadratic curve is a broader algebraic term that also includes some degenerate cases.

examples.everyday: My son is struggling with conic sections in precalc, and he keeps mixing up the ellipse and the circle.
examples.professional: The sensor model fits its signal boundary to a conic section, which makes the fit easy to invert.
examples.analytical: Every conic section is the solution set of a second-degree equation in two variables, which is why the four types form one family.

nuance.analogy: Slicing a cone at different angles is like cutting a carrot with a knife: the cut face is a circle, an oval, a U-shape, or a pair of curves.
nuance.etymology: Conic comes from Greek konikos, 'of a cone,' from konos, 'cone'; section comes from Latin sectio, 'a cutting.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing conic as 'cone-ik,' which sounds like the solid cone and confuses the two words.
Saying 'conical sections' in mathematics, where the correct term is conic sections.

senses.definition: One who conserves, preserves or protects something.
A person appointed by a court to manage the affairs of another; similar to a guardian but with some powers of a trustee.
senses.example: The court appointed a conservator to manage the finances of the elderly widow.

senses.definition: An officer in charge of preserving the public peace, such as a justice or sheriff.
senses.example: The conservator of the peace arrested the drunken men outside the tavern.

senses.definition: A judge delegated by the pope to defend certain privileged classes of persons from manifest or notorious injury or violence, without recourse to a judicial process.
senses.example: The pope named a conservator to protect the pilgrims from violence by local lords.

senses.definition: A professional who works on the conservation and restoration of objects, particularly artistic objects.
senses.example: The museum hired a conservator to clean and stabilize the cracked oil painting.

core.definition: A person who preserves, restores, or protects valuable objects, such as artworks or historic documents.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'SER'. The final syllable is weak and rhotic, so end with a quick American 'er' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and professional; it names a skilled role.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use conservator mainly for museum, art, and archival work, where it is the professional term for someone who restores and protects objects. In legal settings it can also mean a person appointed by a court to manage someone's affairs. In everyday speech, people say restorer or preservationist, or just 'the person who fixes old paintings'.

distinctions.note: Restorer emphasizes repairing damage; conservator emphasizes preventing damage and preserving the object as it is.
Guardian is a general legal or family term for someone caring for a person; conservator in law is specifically appointed by a court to manage property.

examples.everyday: My friend became an art conservator, so she spends her weekends cleaning old family portraits.
examples.professional: The museum hired a textile conservator to stabilize the fragile tapestries before the exhibit.
examples.analytical: The conservator's ethical task is to preserve the artwork's historical evidence rather than to make it look new.

nuance.analogy: A conservator is like a careful doctor for old objects, treating them to slow down decay without changing who they are.
nuance.etymology: From Latin conservator, from conservare, to preserve.
common_mistakes: Confusing conservator with conservative, which is an adjective or noun about political or cautious attitudes.
Using conservator for a repair person in everyday contexts, where restorer is more natural.

conservator.etymology: From Middle English *conservatour*, from Anglo-Norman *conservatour*, from Latin *cōnservātor* (“one who conserves”), agent noun from *cōnservō* (“to preserve”).

senses.definition: Able or likely to be consoled.
senses.example: The grieving child was not easily consolable, so the family took turns sitting with her through the night.

core.definition: Able to be comforted when sad, disappointed or upset. Americans more often use the negative form inconsolable.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on SOH, the second syllable, and the final -able is a weak syllable that sounds like 'bul'. Do not stress the first syllable or pronounce the o as in 'cot'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It describes a person's capacity to be comforted, and it is usually used in contrast with grief or despair.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use consolable in conversation. They are much more likely to say inconsolable, as in 'The baby was inconsolable,' or to say someone 'couldn't be comforted'. You will see consolable in formal writing, letters or literature. A natural everyday reply is simply to ask what happened or offer a hug.

distinctions.note: Inconsolable is the common American form, meaning that someone cannot be comforted at all, while consolable describes the possibility of comfort.
Consolable describes the person who can be comforted, whereas consoling describes the thing or words that give comfort.

examples.professional: Our customers are usually consolable if we explain the delay quickly and give them a clear new date.
examples.analytical: The Stoic writers argued that a wise person is consolable by reason alone, since external goods can always be lost.

nuance.analogy: Like a wound that can heal when it is properly tended, a consolable person can recover from disappointment with the right comfort.
nuance.etymology: From console plus -able; console comes from Latin consolari, 'to comfort'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing console as KON-sole, which is the noun for a panel, instead of kun-SOHL for the verb.
Using consolable in casual speech where Americans would say easy to comfort or inconsolable.

senses.definition: To secretly plot or make plans together, often with the intention to bring bad or illegal results; to collude, to connive, to plot.
senses.example: The two former employees conspired to steal trade secrets and sell them overseas.

senses.definition: To agree, to concur to one end.
senses.example: Several unlikely factors conspired to make the storm's damage worse than predicted.

senses.definition: To work together to bring about.
senses.example: Rain and sweat conspired to smudge her mascara.

core.definition: To plan secretly with others to do something harmful or illegal, or to act together toward a common end.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SPYE, the second syllable. The final -ire is pronounced as a single rhotic syllable, like the -er in butter, not as a separate syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative in crime contexts, but playful when things seem to work together by chance, as in 'everything conspired to make the day perfect.'
nuance.usage_note: Americans use conspire for crimes and political plots, and humorously for events that seem to join forces. It is usually followed by to plus a verb: 'they conspired to rob the bank.' In everyday talk, plot or scheme is more common, so conspire can sound a little formal or dramatic.

distinctions.note: Collude stresses secret cooperation, often in business or politics, usually to cheat others; conspire focuses on a joint plan, often criminal.
Scheme suggests clever or sometimes petty planning; conspire implies a group plan aimed at a serious end.

examples.everyday: My sisters conspired to plan my birthday party, and I didn't suspect a thing.
examples.professional: The two vendors appear to have conspired on their bids, so we are referring the case to compliance.
examples.analytical: Psalm 2:1 asks why the nations conspire in vain, placing human plotting under God's sovereignty.

nuance.analogy: Like many threads pulled together to weave one cloth, which can be a beautiful gift or a trap.
nuance.etymology: From Latin conspirare, 'to agree, plot together', from con- 'together' and spirare 'to breathe'.
common_mistakes: Using conspire without to before the verb, as in 'they conspired steal the money'.
Confusing conspire with inspire, which has a very different meaning.
Stressing the first syllable instead of the second: kun-SPYE-er, not KON-spire.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew verb rāgaš, translated conspire in Psalm 2:1 of the RSV, means to rage or plot together. Psalm 2 describes earthly rulers gathering against the LORD and his anointed, and the psalm shows that such plotting is futile. Acts 4:25-27 quotes this theme and applies it to the opposition to Jesus. The passage reminds readers that human conspiracies cannot overturn God's purposes.

conspire.etymology: From Middle English *conspiren*, from Old French *conspirer*, from Latin *conspirare*, *conspīrō*, from *con-* (combining form of *cum* (“with”)) + *spīrō* (“breathe”).

senses.definition: Unchanged through time or space; permanent.
senses.example: Her love for her grandmother remained constant throughout the years of illness.

senses.definition: Consistently recurring over time; persistent.
senses.example: The constant ringing of the phone gave him a headache all morning.

senses.definition: Steady in purpose, action, feeling, etc.
senses.example: She was a constant friend who never wavered during my hardest months.

senses.definition: Firm; solid; not fluid.
senses.example: Hikers prefer a surface that stays constant underfoot rather than soft mud.

senses.definition: Bounded above by a constant.
senses.example: constant time constant space

senses.definition: That which is permanent or invariable.
senses.example: For the theologian, God remains the one constant in an uncertain world.

senses.definition: A quantity that remains at a fixed value throughout a given discussion or operation.
senses.example: In the equation y = mx + b, the value of b is a constant.

senses.definition: Any property of an experiment, determined numerically, that does not change under given circumstances.
senses.example: Our simulation kept the learning rate constant, so the only variable was batch size.

senses.definition: An identifier that is bound to an invariant value; a fixed value given a name to aid in readability of source code.
senses.example: Declare the maximum retry count as a constant so nobody changes it accidentally.

core.definition: Never changing or stopping; continuous, or steady and repeated over time.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, KON. The second syllable is reduced to a short 'stunt', so do not say 'kon-STANT' or pronounce the 'a' as 'ah'. In General American the o in cot and the a in caught sound the same.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive when describing stability, support or loyalty. Negative when describing an annoying repetition, such as constant interruptions.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use constant in everyday speech for something that never stops, like constant noise or a constant reminder, and in professional talk for steady conditions. A friend who is a constant support is a compliment. Use it with a noun, and use constantly for the adverb.

distinctions.note: Continuous means without any break in time or space; constant means steady or repeated, with the same character over time.
Consistent describes a pattern that matches across cases; constant describes something that persists or recurs over time.

examples.everyday: My little brother has a constant stream of questions when we drive.
examples.professional: We need a constant data feed for the model, not a daily batch, or the forecasts will drift.
examples.analytical: If the speed of light is treated as a constant, the theory's structure depends on that assumption being stable across frames of reference.

nuance.analogy: A constant is like the North Star: it stays fixed while everything else in the sky seems to move around it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin constans, 'standing firm', from constare, 'to stand firm'.
common_mistakes: Using the adjective for the adverb: say 'He is constantly late', not 'He is constant late'.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'kon-STANT'.
Pronouncing the middle vowel as a full 'ah' sound; it is reduced.

constant.etymology: From Middle English *constant*, from Old French *constant*, from Latin *constantem*, accusative of *constans*, from *consto* (“to stand firm”).

senses.definition: Conducted without human-to-human contact so as to reduce the potential spread of a contagious disease.

core.definition: Done without physical touching between people, to reduce the spread of a contagious disease.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FREE, the main beat, and contact has a weaker secondary stress on its first syllable, KON. In phrases the final t of contact often softens into the next word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It describes a safe or hygienic process, though in some settings it sounds clinical.
nuance.usage_note: Americans used contact-free widely during the COVID-19 pandemic for pickup, payment, and check-in. Stores and restaurants still use it for tap-to-pay and delivery. You can also say contactless, which is common in payment contexts such as contactless cards.

distinctions.note: Contact-free and contactless are often interchangeable, but contactless is more common for payment cards, while contact-free is more common for services and procedures.
No-touch is more casual and informal; contact-free sounds more official, like a public health notice.

examples.everyday: Most stores still offer contact-free pickup, so you can grab your order from the curb without going inside.
examples.professional: We moved the check-in process to a contact-free kiosk so the front desk staff are safer during flu season.
examples.analytical: A contact-free protocol reduces the risk of transmission, but it cannot eliminate that risk entirely.

nuance.analogy: A contact-free process is like a screen door: it lets the service through while keeping the hands apart.
nuance.etymology: Compound of contact (from Latin contactus) and free (from Old English freo).
common_mistakes: Saying contact free without a hyphen in formal writing; the hyphen is standard before a noun.
Stressing contact as the main beat; the strongest stress is on free.

senses.definition: Of or in counterpoint.
Of or relating to counterpoint.
With two or more independent melodic lines.

core.definition: Relating to counterpoint, the writing of two or more independent melodic lines that sound good together.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on PUN, and the first syllable keeps a secondary stress. Americans give the final syllable a light, reduced vowel, so avoid saying a full 'tal'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a musical or structural technique and can be a mild compliment when praising complex, well-woven writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in music theory, music criticism, and academic discussions of composition, such as talking about Bach fugues. In everyday speech, people would say 'complex' or 'interwoven' instead. Outside music, it is sometimes used figuratively for two independent threads that interact well, but this is less common.

distinctions.note: Harmonic describes music organized by vertical chords; contrapuntal describes music organized by horizontal, independent melodic lines.
Polyphonic is broader and means many voices or parts sounding together; contrapuntal refers specifically to the technique of combining those lines according to rules.

examples.everyday: My brother plays the organ, and he says Bach's fugues are so contrapuntal that you can follow every voice.
examples.professional: The arrangement is very contrapuntal, so we need to make sure the bass line doesn't get buried under the vocal melody.
examples.analytical: Bach's late works reveal a contrapuntal logic in which each voice keeps its own contour while still belonging to the whole.

nuance.analogy: Like two people telling different stories at once that still fit together into one conversation.
nuance.etymology: From Italian contrappunto, meaning point against point, referring to placing one note against another.
common_mistakes: Using it for any disagreement or argument; it is limited to music and similar structures.
Stressing the wrong syllable as kahn-TRUH-pun-tul.

contrapuntal.etymology: From Latin *punctus contra punctum* (“note against note”).

senses.definition: A flat, usually vertical surface onto which controls, instruments, and displays are mounted.
senses.example: The pilot checked the control panel before lifting the aircraft off the runway.

senses.definition: A computer display offering a number of controls or options.
senses.example: The software's control panel lets administrators change user permissions with a few clicks.

core.definition: A flat surface holding the buttons, switches, and displays used to operate a machine or system.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first word on TROHL and the second on PAN, and the second syllable of panel is a reduced vowel, so it sounds like 'PAN-uhl'. Americans link the words so it sounds like 'kun-TROHL-PAN-uhl'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and descriptive, with no positive or negative shift.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use control panel for a physical board of buttons and dials, such as in a car, a factory, a thermostat wall unit, or an airplane cockpit. In everyday speech, it is also used for a computer's settings window, as in 'Open the Control Panel' on Windows. It is not used for a single button, which would be called a switch or a button.

distinctions.note: A dashboard usually refers to the display in front of a driver, while a control panel can be any surface of controls, including industrial and home equipment.
A console is a freestanding unit or desk with controls, while a control panel is usually a flat surface mounted on a wall or machine.

examples.everyday: Can you press the blue button on the control panel near the door so the garage opens?
examples.professional: The engineer checked the control panel readings before approving the restart of the line.
examples.analytical: The control panel is a design interface that mediates between human intention and machine behavior, so its layout shapes what operators can understand and do.

nuance.analogy: Like the cockpit of an airplane, where every switch and gauge gives the pilot a way to direct the machine.
nuance.etymology: Control (from Anglo-French contreroller) combined with panel (from Old French panel, 'a piece of cloth' or 'a flat section').
common_mistakes: Stressing 'panel' like 'pan-EL'; in American speech the stress lands on PAN and the ending is reduced.
Using 'control panel' for a single button or lever, which Americans would call a control or switch.

Pronouncing 'control' with a British-style 'con-TROHL' stress on the second syllable only in a compound phrase; the stress is the same, but the second element often takes the stress in running speech.

senses.definition: One who cooperates; an associate.
senses.example: She was a loyal cooperator on the project, sharing data and helping test every model.

core.definition: A person who works with others toward a shared goal; a partner or collaborator in an effort.

pronunciation.tip: Keep the final syllable as an American r-colored 'tur'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It describes a participant in a joint effort, often in research, agriculture, or formal arrangements.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use cooperator mostly in formal or technical contexts, such as research studies, agricultural cooperatives, or legal and administrative documents. In everyday speech, people say 'partner,' 'teammate,' or 'collaborator.' It can sound stiff if used casually.

distinctions.note: A collaborator usually creates something jointly, often as an equal. A cooperator is more formal and can mean any participant who helps.
Partner is common and warm. Cooperator is formal and suggests a participant in an arrangement.

examples.everyday: Thanks for being such a good cooperator while we sorted out the parking problem.
examples.professional: As a cooperator in the study, she agreed to share her anonymized records with the research team.
examples.analytical: The philosopher treats each citizen as a cooperator in a shared social project rather than as a mere subject of the state.

nuance.analogy: A cooperator is like a rope partner on a climbing team: the rope only works if both people do their part.
nuance.etymology: From cooperate plus the agent suffix -or, from Latin co- 'together' and operari 'to work.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable as koh-oh-PAR-ay-ter; the main stress is on the second syllable AH.
