core.definition: The process by which the body breaks down food into substances it can absorb and use.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, JES, and the first syllable sounds like 'dye'. The -tion ending is pronounced 'chun' with a ch sound, not 'shun'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In everyday talk it is often used with 'good' or 'bad' to describe how someone's stomach handles food, which can be negative in context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'digestion' in casual talk about stomach problems, meals and health, as in 'my digestion is bad.' It is also standard in medical and nutrition writing. In everyday speech people often say 'stomach' or 'digestive problems' instead, but 'digestion' is always natural.

distinctions.note: Indigestion is the discomfort or pain after eating; digestion is the normal process itself.
Absorption is the step where nutrients pass through the intestinal wall into the blood, which happens after digestion breaks food down.
Metabolism covers all the chemical reactions in the body, including those that happen after nutrients are absorbed.

examples.everyday: I always feel sluggish after a big lunch because my digestion just slows way down.
examples.professional: The nutrition team's report on digestion recommended more fiber for our meal-kit customers.
examples.analytical: Digestion is best understood as a chain of enzymatic and mechanical processes, each of which can fail independently.

nuance.analogy: Think of digestion as a factory line that breaks raw materials into smaller parts the rest of the plant can use.
nuance.etymology: From Latin digestio, from digerere 'to divide, dissolve,' from dis- 'apart' plus gerere 'to carry.'
common_mistakes: Reducing the first syllable to 'dih-JES-chun'; the first syllable is stressed and sounds like 'dye'.
Confusing digestion with indigestion: indigestion is the problem, while digestion is the normal process.

senses.definition: Short for Dijon mustard.

core.definition: Short for Dijon mustard: a smooth, sharp French-style mustard that Americans often just call Dijon at the table or in recipes.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, -ZHAHN, with a French-style zh sound in the middle. It is not 'DYE-jon' or 'DIJ-un'; the vowel at the end is an American 'ah'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests a good-quality condiment and sounds casual and friendly in everyday speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often shorten Dijon mustard to Dijon, as in can you pass the Dijon? or a little Dijon on the sandwich. In most stores it is in the condiment aisle near yellow mustard. Dijon is also the name of the city in Burgundy, but in everyday American speech the word usually means the mustard.

distinctions.note: Yellow mustard is the mild, bright ballpark-style condiment; Dijon is smoother, sharper and more pungent.
Whole-grain mustard has visible seeds and a coarse texture; Dijon is smooth, though grainy Dijon varieties also exist.

examples.everyday: Can you grab the Dijon from the fridge? I want to whip up a quick vinaigrette for the salad.
examples.professional: The catering order includes two jars of Dijon for the sandwich bar at the lunch meeting.
examples.analytical: The name Dijon now signals a style of mustard more than a place, since much of what American shelves label Dijon is made far from Burgundy.

nuance.analogy: Dijon is to mustard what a sharp cheddar is to cheese: a named style that tells you what kind of bite to expect.
nuance.etymology: Named after Dijon, the city in Burgundy, France, where this style of mustard developed.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it DYE-jon or DIJ-un; the correct stress is dee-ZHAHN.
Using Dijon to mean any mustard, when Americans may ask for yellow mustard if they want the mild kind.

dijon.etymology: French *Dijon*, from the Roman name, Latin *Diviō*, from the name *Divius* (“godly, divine”); see *divus*.

senses.definition: In a disappointing manner.
senses.example: I spent countless hours revising, but, disappointingly, I still failed the exam.

core.definition: In a way that is less good than someone expected or hoped; used to describe a result or quality that fell short.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on POYN, not on the first syllable. Do not add an extra vowel before the final -ly: the ending is ting-lee, two clear syllables.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a letdown with a mild, often polite tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use disappointingly to comment on results, service, or performance: 'The service was disappointingly slow.' It is often used as a polite criticism in reviews and meetings. A natural reply is 'Yeah, I expected better too.'

distinctions.note: Unfortunately introduces bad news without judging quality; disappointingly judges something as falling short of expectations.
Sadly expresses sorrow, while disappointingly expresses a letdown about performance or results.
Surprisingly signals that something was unexpected in any direction; disappointingly always signals a negative letdown.

examples.everyday: The pizza was disappointingly cold by the time it reached our table.
examples.professional: Sales were disappointingly flat in the third quarter, so we are reviewing the marketing plan.
examples.analytical: The experiment disappointingly failed to replicate the earlier finding, which undermines the strength of the original claim.

nuance.analogy: Like a cake that looks perfect on the plate but is dry inside: the expectation was high, and the result fell short.
nuance.etymology: From disappointing plus the adverb suffix -ly; see disappoint, from Old French desappointer.
common_mistakes: Putting the stress on the first syllable; the main stress is on POYN.
Using disappointingly to describe a person's feelings; use disappointed for feelings.

senses.definition: Impolite; lacking consideration for others.

core.definition: Impolite, lacking consideration or basic respect for others.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KUR, the second syllable, with the American 'ur' vowel and a clear r. The ending 'tee-us' is two light syllables, so do not say 'dis-KUR-shus' or 'dis-KOR-tee-ous'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It criticizes behavior that lacks basic courtesy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use discourteous in formal writing, complaints, reviews and careful speech, as in 'The staff was discourteous.' In casual speech they usually say 'rude' or 'not nice'. Because it sounds more formal than 'rude', it can be used in a polite letter or a calm complaint.

distinctions.note: Rude is blunt and common and often stronger; discourteous is more formal and measured, often used in writing.
Unkind is about harmful intent or cruelty; discourteous is about a lack of basic courtesy or consideration.

examples.everyday: The cashier was discourteous and never even looked up when I said thank you.
examples.professional: Replying to a client's email with one word is discourteous, even if you are busy.
examples.analytical: To call an opponent's argument stupid is discourteous, whatever its merits.

nuance.analogy: Like a door let swing shut in someone's face rather than held open for them.
nuance.etymology: From Old French descourtois, from des- (not) plus courtois (courteous).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with 'or' as in 'dis-COR-tee-us'; the vowel is the American 'ur' sound.
Using 'discourteous' for a single small mistake; it describes a pattern of behavior.

senses.definition: Lack of courtesy; rudeness.
A rude act.

core.definition: Rude behavior or a lack of politeness; an act or remark that shows a lack of courtesy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, with a weaker secondary stress on -cour-. The final -tesy is reduced to 'tuh-see', not 'TEE-see'. Keep the r in the middle syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It names rudeness in a measured, somewhat formal way, so it sounds milder than 'rudeness' or 'being a jerk'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'discourtesy' more in writing, formal complaints, or polite criticism than in casual talk. In speech, 'rude' or 'rudeness' is more natural. A typical reply to an apology is 'No worries' or 'It's fine'.

distinctions.note: Rudeness is the everyday word and can be stronger; discourtesy is more formal and often describes a single, relatively minor act.
Impoliteness is a broader, more neutral term for failing to observe social norms; discourtesy implies a deliberate or careless slight.
An insult is an act meant to offend directly; a discourtesy may be unintentional, such as ignoring someone who is speaking.

examples.everyday: I was annoyed by the discourtesy of the cashier who never looked up from her phone.
examples.professional: Interrupting clients during calls is a discourtesy we should train out of the whole team.
examples.analytical: Erasmus wrote that a small discourtesy can wound a friendship more than a large injury, because it signals indifference.

nuance.analogy: Like a small scratch on a car door: no single scratch ruins the car, but many of them change how it looks.
nuance.etymology: From dis- (not, lacking) and courtesy, from Old French cortoisie, related to court, the behavior expected at a royal court.
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable as 'dis-cour-TEE-see'; the stress belongs on the first syllable.
Using 'discourtesy' for a big, angry insult in casual speech, where 'rude' fits better.

senses.definition: In AI: In a GAN, the network that tries to tell real samples from generated ones.
A person who discriminates, as:
senses.example: keen discriminator

senses.definition: A person who differentiates things or concepts.
senses.example: keen discriminator

senses.definition: A person who acts unfairly through prejudice.
senses.example: I am not a discriminator

senses.definition: A test or variable, etc. that serves to distinguish between different things.
senses.example: Color is not an effective discriminator when it comes to the spiciness of food.

senses.definition: A feature of the seller's offering that differs from a competitor's offering and is important to the buyer in question.
senses.example: An especially strong warranty can be a discriminator in some marketplaces.

senses.definition: Any of several electronic devices that convert some property of a signal into an amplitude whose value is proportional to the difference between the value of the input signal and that of a standard.
senses.example: The engineers replaced the old comparator with a discriminator to sort pulses by amplitude.

core.definition: In AI, the network in a GAN that learns to tell real data samples apart from generated, fake ones.

pronunciation.tip: Stress SKRIM, the second syllable. The final '-or' is a reduced American 'er' sound, so say 'ter' with a flat, rhotic r, not 'tor'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. In general English it can refer to a person who discriminates, but that use is uncommon.
nuance.usage_note: In American technical English, discriminator is standard in machine learning, especially in discussions of generative adversarial networks, where it is paired with the generator. Outside that field it is rare, and an American would normally say 'someone who discriminates' or 'a biased person' for the social sense. Engineers often shorten it informally to 'the discriminator' in conversation.

distinctions.note: In a GAN the generator creates fake samples while the discriminator judges whether a sample is real or fake.
A classifier assigns inputs to classes in general, while a discriminator specifically judges real versus generated data in a GAN.

examples.everyday: My friend who works in AI says the discriminator in their image model got so good that the generator kept failing to fool it.
examples.professional: If the discriminator becomes too strong, the generator gets almost no useful gradient, so we need to monitor the discriminator loss during training.
examples.analytical: The discriminator in a GAN defines an implicit objective, and its equilibrium with the generator determines whether the learned distribution matches the data.

nuance.analogy: The discriminator is like a counterfeit-money inspector who gets better and better at spotting fakes, which forces the counterfeiter to produce more convincing bills.
nuance.etymology: From discriminate, with the agent suffix -or, from Latin discriminare, 'to separate, distinguish.'
common_mistakes: Using discriminator to mean someone who treats people unfairly, which is not the usual American meaning.
Confusing the discriminator with the generator, since in a GAN they play opposite roles.

conversation.text: The discriminator learns to tell real samples from the generator's fakes.
If the discriminator gets too strong too fast, the generator stops getting useful gradients.

senses.definition: To free something from entanglement; to extricate or unknot.
senses.example: I had to disentangle him from his own shoelaces.

senses.definition: To unravel; to separate into discrete components or units.
senses.example: It took an hour to disentangle the Christmas lights without breaking any of the bulbs.

senses.definition: To become free or untangled.
senses.example: The kitten finally disentangled itself from the yarn and bounced off across the room.

core.definition: To free something or someone from a tangle, complication or involvement, or to sort out a confusing situation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TANG, the second syllable of tangle, and the final -le is a syllabic l with no full vowel after the g. The first syllables dis and in are unstressed.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it describes careful work to separate things that have become mixed up or complicated.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use disentangle for literal things like fishing line, cords or hair, and figuratively for relationships, legal problems, finances or confusing arguments. It sounds a little more polished than untangle, which is the everyday word for knots and cords. In business talk someone might say 'We need to disentangle the two accounts,' and a colleague would reply 'Let's do it this week.'

distinctions.note: Untangle is more everyday and usually refers to physical knots like cords or hair; disentangle is more formal and often used for complex or figurative tangles.
Extricate stresses freeing someone from a trap or dangerous situation; disentangle more often means sorting out a mixed-up or complicated thing.

examples.everyday: It took me twenty minutes to disentangle the Christmas lights, but they finally work.
examples.professional: We need to disentangle the billing errors from the contract dispute before the audit next week.
examples.analytical: The author tries to disentangle the moral and political motives that were tangled together in the reform movement.

nuance.analogy: Disentangling a problem is like working a knot out of a necklace: you loosen each strand slowly until the chain lies flat.
nuance.etymology: From dis- (reversal) plus entangle, from en- and tangle, probably of Scandinavian origin.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable: DIS-en-tangle
Giving the final -gle a full vowel, as in 'gleh'; it is a syllabic l

senses.definition: A decrease in the inflation rate.
Deflation.
senses.example: Economists feared that the disinflation would deepen into outright deflation, cutting wages and spending sharply.

core.definition: A slowing of the rate of inflation, meaning prices still rise but more slowly; it is not the same as prices falling.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the FLAY syllable, which is the main vowel of the word, and the final -tion is shun.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a technical economic condition, often discussed in news about central banks.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use disinflation in economics, finance, and news about the Federal Reserve when inflation is falling but not yet negative. Ordinary speakers more often say inflation is coming down or prices are rising more slowly. The word can confuse people, so explain it as slower inflation, not falling prices.

distinctions.note: Deflation means prices actually fall; disinflation means the rate of price increase slows but prices still rise.
Inflation is rising prices overall; disinflation is a slowdown in that rise.

examples.everyday: The news says inflation is slowing, which economists call disinflation, but grocery prices are still higher than last year.
examples.professional: Our finance team expects disinflation to continue this year, so we are holding the pricing increase.
examples.analytical: Disinflation can occur without deflation, and distinguishing the two is essential for interpreting monetary policy.

nuance.analogy: Like a car easing off the gas: it is still moving forward, just more slowly.
nuance.etymology: From dis- (reversing) plus inflation, from Latin inflare, to blow into.
common_mistakes: Thinking disinflation means prices fall, which is deflation
Stressing the first syllable as in DIS-in-flay-shun
Using disinflation in casual speech where slowing inflation is clearer

senses.definition: One of multiple propositions, any of which, if true, confirm the validity of another proposition (a disjunction).
The state of being disjointed; disjointedness; a disconnect.
Any sentence element that is not fully integrated into the clausal structure of the sentence.
senses.example: The parenthetical 'by the way' in her sentence is a disjunct, set apart from the main clause by commas.

senses.definition: An adverbial that expresses the speaker's or writer's attitude towards, or descriptive statement of, the propositional content of the associated clause or sentence.
senses.example: Frankly, the disjunct at the start of his email signaled that he was annoyed.

senses.definition: A species or population occurring at a distant or separate location, and separated from other members of the same group.
senses.example: The botanist recorded a disjunct population of the orchid, hundreds of miles from its nearest relatives.

senses.definition: (rare) A conjunct of a disjunctive conjunction.
senses.example: In the sentence 'either we leave or we stay', each disjunct is a full clause.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: Separate; discontinuous; not connected.
senses.example: The disjunct parts of the manuscript were scattered across three libraries and never reunited.

senses.definition: Occurring in widely separated geographic areas.
senses.example: The fossil record shows disjunct ranges for these salamanders, which once lived in both Ohio and Japan.

core.definition: In logic, one of the alternatives in a disjunction; one of the propositions joined by or, any of which can be true.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on JUNK, the second syllable. Keep the ending hard with a clear kt sound, and make the vowel in the middle short.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical term used in formal logic and linguistics.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use disjunct almost only in logic, philosophy, and linguistics classes. In general conversation the word is unfamiliar, and people say separate or disconnected. Use it with care in academic writing, where it has a precise meaning.

distinctions.note: A disjunct is one of the parts joined by or; a disjunction is the whole compound statement made of those parts.
A conjunct is one of the parts joined by and; a disjunct is one of the parts joined by or.

examples.everyday: I'm not sure, but I think the second option is the disjunct that matters for this puzzle.
examples.professional: In the rule engine, each disjunct is a separate condition, and the request is approved if any one of them is true.
examples.analytical: If one disjunct is false, the truth of the whole disjunction depends entirely on the remaining disjunct, which is what makes the inference valid.

nuance.analogy: A disjunct is one of several doors into a room; any one of them being open gets you in.
nuance.etymology: From Latin disjunctus, past participle of disjungere, 'to separate'.
common_mistakes: Using disjunct as a general word for separated things in everyday speech.
Confusing disjunct with conjunct, which is the and version.

senses.definition: An act of being disloyal; a betrayal, faithbreach.
The quality of being disloyal.

core.definition: The quality of not being loyal, or an act of betraying a person, group, country or cause.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on LOY, and the middle syllable is a reduced, nearly silent 'uhl'. Many Americans say the l as a syllabic sound, so it is 'dis-LOY-l-tee'. The final syllable is 'tee'.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. It implies betrayal, disrespect or a broken commitment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use disloyalty to describe betrayal in the workplace, in politics and among friends, as in 'accusations of disloyalty' or 'a sign of disloyalty.' It is more formal than 'betrayal' in casual speech and sounds more serious than 'not being on my side'. In a conversation, 'that's disloyalty' is a strong and direct statement.

distinctions.note: Betrayal often describes a specific act that hurts someone who trusted you; disloyalty can be a quality or a pattern of behavior.
Infidelity usually means sexual unfaithfulness in a relationship; disloyalty is broader and covers friends, teams, employers and countries.

examples.everyday: My friend told everyone my secret, and I just can't get past that kind of disloyalty.
examples.professional: Several managers raised concerns about disloyalty when the sales data was leaked to a competitor.
examples.analytical: Josiah Royce treated loyalty as the root of moral life, so he saw disloyalty not merely as a personal failing but as a breakdown of the community that shapes a self.

nuance.analogy: Like a bridge with one support cable removed: it may still stand for a while, but the trust that holds it up has been damaged.
nuance.etymology: From disloyal, plus the noun suffix -ty, from Old French loialte.
common_mistakes: Confusing the noun with 'disloyal' as an adjective, as in 'the disloyal of the employee' instead of 'the employee's disloyalty'.
Stressing the first syllable as in DIS-loy-al-ty; the stress is on LOY.
Using 'disloyalty' for mild disagreement; it implies betrayal of a commitment.

senses.definition: To terminate a union of multiple members actively, as by disbanding.
senses.example: The ruling party or coalition sometimes dissolves parliament early when the polls are favorable, hoping to reconvene with a larger majority.

senses.definition: To destroy, make disappear.
To liquify, melt into a fluid.
To be melted, changed into a fluid.
To disperse, drive apart a group of persons.
To break the continuity of; to disconnect; to loosen; to undo; to separate.
To shift from one shot to another by having the former fade out as the latter fades in.
To resolve itself as by dissolution.
To relax by pleasure; to make powerless.
To separate a ligature into its component letters.
To disintegrate chemically into a solution by immersion into a liquid or other material.
To be disintegrated by such immersion.
To annul; to rescind; to discharge or release.
senses.example: to dissolve an injunction

senses.definition: A form of film punctuation in which there is a gradual transition from one scene to the next.

core.definition: To mix into a liquid until it disappears, or to end a formal group, agreement, or relationship.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, and the s sounds like a z. The final l is usually light and often almost silent, so say dih-ZAHLV, not dih-ZOLV-ed.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can describe physical change, a formal ending, or a fading away, depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English, people use dissolve for sugar or powder in water, and for a meeting or partnership that officially ends. Dissolve can also describe a scene in a film that fades into another. It is less dramatic than break down and more formal than end.

distinctions.note: Melt describes solids becoming liquid because of heat; dissolve describes a solid becoming part of a liquid, even at room temperature.
Disband is used mainly for groups, such as bands or military units, while dissolve can also apply to legal bodies and relationships.

examples.everyday: Stir the powder into your coffee and wait until it dissolves completely.
examples.professional: The board voted to dissolve the working group once the migration project is finished.
examples.analytical: Hume argues that the self can dissolve under analysis into a bundle of perceptions, not a single enduring substance.

nuance.analogy: Dissolving is like sugar in tea: the solid still exists, but it is no longer visible as separate pieces.
nuance.etymology: From Latin dissolvere, meaning to loosen apart or unbind.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final l, as in dih-ZOLV-ed; the l is usually silent in American speech.
Using dissolve for a person's emotional breakdown, where break down is more natural.

senses.definition: Lacking unity; not united.
senses.example: The two rival committees remained disunited, arguing over every budget line through the entire meeting.

core.definition: Not joined together; divided in opinion, purpose, or loyalty, so that people do not act as one.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the syllable NY, as in 'unite', not the first syllable. The ending -ed is pronounced as 'id' here because it follows the t sound in 'unite'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a lack of unity that weakens a group.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'disunited' in political, historical, and formal contexts, such as 'a disunited party' or 'a disunited front'. In everyday speech they more often say 'divided' or 'not on the same page'. It is a serious word, so avoid it for small disagreements.

distinctions.note: 'Divided' is common and neutral, while 'disunited' emphasizes a lack of cohesion or shared purpose.
'Fragmented' suggests something broken into many small pieces, and it is common in technical writing about systems or data.

examples.everyday: Our neighborhood association was pretty disunited about the new parking rules, so nothing got decided.
examples.professional: The leadership team looked disunited in front of the board, which weakened the proposal.
examples.analytical: A disunited opposition cannot offer voters a credible alternative to the government's program.

nuance.analogy: A disunited group is like an orchestra where each musician plays a different piece: the sounds are there, but they do not make music together.
nuance.etymology: From disunite, the verb, plus the adjectival ending -ed.
common_mistakes: Using 'disunity' (the noun) where the adjective 'disunited' is needed, as in 'a disunity party'.
Stressing the first syllable instead of the NY syllable.

senses.definition: Consisting of different elements; various.
senses.example: The museum displays a diverse collection of pottery, textiles, and tools from many cultures.

senses.definition: Capable of or having various forms in different situations or at different times; multiform.
senses.example: Amphibian larvae are diverse in form, adapting to ponds, streams, and even puddles.

senses.definition: Chiefly preceded by a descriptive word: of a community, organization, etc.: composed of people with a variety of different demographic characteristics such as ethnicity, gender, sexual orientation, or socioeconomic status; especially, having a sizeable representation of people who are minorities in the community, organization, etc.
senses.example: The startup says its engineering team is racially diverse, though leadership remains mostly male.

senses.definition: Not the same; different, dissimilar, distinct.
senses.example: Our two sisters have diverse tastes, so they never agree on which movie to watch.

senses.definition: Differing from what is good or right, or beneficial; bad, evil; harmful.
senses.example: Such diverse counsels from the wicked king led his people into ruin.

senses.definition: Having different colors; mottled, variegated.
senses.example: The diverse plumage of the tropical bird dazzled the tourists on the trail.

senses.definition: (rare) Causing one to be indecisive between different viewpoints.
senses.example: The evidence was so diverse that the jury could not settle on one conclusion.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: Synonym of diversely (“in different directions”).
senses.example: The seeds blew diverse across the field, carried by winds from every direction.

senses.definition: Synonym of diversify.
senses.example: The company wants to diverse its revenue by entering healthcare and logistics.

senses.definition: To make (something) different or varied in form or quality; to alter, to change, to vary.
senses.example: Cooks often diverse a basic recipe with spices, herbs, or seasonal vegetables.

senses.definition: To make the scope of (business, investments, etc.) different or varied, especially so as to balance and mitigate risks.
senses.example: Financial advisers urge retirees to diverse their portfolios to reduce risk.

core.definition: Made up of many different kinds of people, things, or ideas; varied.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, and do not pronounce it 'dih-VERSE' with a short e; the vowel is the r-colored 'ur' sound. The final s is voiceless, like 'bus', not a z.

nuance.connotation: Positive in most American contexts, since diversity is generally valued. It can sound neutral or technical in other settings, such as describing species or data.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use diverse constantly for workplaces, neighborhoods, menus, and teams: 'It's a really diverse neighborhood.' In the US the word often refers to people from different ethnic, racial, or cultural backgrounds, so be careful when describing a group. For a list of options, 'a diverse range of' sounds natural in both writing and speech.

distinctions.note: Various stresses a number of separate items; diverse adds the idea that the items are clearly different in kind.
Different is a plain comparison between two things, while diverse suggests a broad mix within one group or set.

examples.everyday: Our neighborhood is pretty diverse, so you hear a lot of different languages at the farmers market.
examples.professional: We want our hiring panel to be more diverse, so please include candidates from outside our usual schools.
examples.analytical: A diverse community of interpreters can reveal readings of a text that a single tradition would overlook.

nuance.analogy: Like a well-mixed salad, where each ingredient keeps its own flavor and the whole is richer for the mix.
nuance.etymology: From Latin diversus, 'turned in different directions', past participle of divertere.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the word as 'dih-VERSE' with a short e instead of the r-colored 'ur' vowel.
Confusing diverse (adjective) with diversity (noun): 'a diverse team' is correct, not 'a diversity team' for the same meaning.

diverse.etymology: The adjective is derived from Middle English *divers*, *diverse* (“different, divergent”), from Anglo-Norman *divers*, Anglo-Norman *divers*, and Old French *divers* (“different; of various kinds”), and directly from their etymon Latin *dīversus*…

senses.definition: Initialism of do it yourself.
senses.example: We saved hundreds of dollars by doing the bathroom remodel as a DIY project.

senses.definition: To perform oneself a task usually relegated to an expert.
senses.example: I decided to DIY the kitchen cabinets instead of hiring a contractor.

senses.definition: Do-it-yourself.
senses.example: Do you know where I could find a DIY pipe repair kit?

core.definition: Projects or repairs that people do themselves, without hiring a professional.

pronunciation.tip: Americans say the letters D, I, and Y one at a time, not as a word. Stress the final 'why' sound most strongly, and make the middle 'eye' clearly separate.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests self-reliance, creativity, and saving money, though it can imply skill is needed.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use DIY for home repairs, crafts, and projects, as in 'a DIY kitchen remodel' or 'Let's do it DIY.' It is informal but widely understood. Avoid saying 'DIY' for work that really requires licensed professionals, such as electrical work in many states.
word_family: DIYer (noun, a person who does DIY)

distinctions.note: A handyman is a paid worker who fixes things for others, while DIY describes doing the work yourself.
A contractor is a licensed professional who manages construction, whereas DIY work is done by the owner or a volunteer.

examples.everyday: We did most of the bathroom ourselves, so it was a DIY job from start to finish.
examples.professional: The DIY dashboard prototype my intern built is good enough for Monday's review.
examples.analytical: The rise of DIY culture reflects a broader skepticism toward expert authority in everyday life.

nuance.analogy: DIY is like cooking at home instead of ordering takeout: you take on the work yourself to save money and learn something.
nuance.etymology: Initialism of 'do it yourself', first common in American and British usage in the mid-20th century.
common_mistakes: Say the letters separately: 'dee-eye-WHY', not 'DIE' or 'dee-EYE'.
Do not confuse 'DIY' with 'homemade' when you mean a skilled professional's work.

related: DIYer (noun, a person who does DIY)

do-you-have-any-bags-to-check.phonetic: /du ju hæv ˌɛni ˌbæɡz tu ˈtʃɛk/

senses.definition: An airline agent asking whether you have luggage for the plane's hold.

core.definition: An airline agent's question asking whether you have luggage that should go into the plane's cargo hold rather than stay with you.

pronunciation.respelling: doo yoo hav en-ee bagz too CHEK
pronunciation.tip: In speech, 'any' is usually reduced to 'nee' and 'to' to 'tuh', so the phrase sounds like 'doo yoo hav nee bagz tuh CHEK'. The stress falls on 'check', and the 'ch' sound is the one to focus on.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a standard procedural question at airports.
nuance.usage_note: Airline agents and check-in staff use this at the counter or the kiosk. A typical answer is 'Yes, one bag' or 'No, just this carry-on.' Americans also say 'checked bag' for the bag that goes into the hold.

distinctions.note: A carry-on stays with you in the cabin; a bag to check goes into the hold and is handled by the airline.
'Check in' means to register for a flight; 'check' as in 'check a bag' means to hand over luggage for the hold.

examples.everyday: Do you have any bags to check, or just the backpack?
examples.professional: Do you have any bags to check for the flight, or will everything go in the overhead bin?
examples.analytical: The agent's question sorts travelers into those who accept a delay in exchange for carrying no luggage and those who must surrender their bags to the hold.

nuance.analogy: Like handing your coat to a coat check at a restaurant: you give up the bag and get it back at the destination.
common_mistakes: Saying 'check the bags' when you mean to ask whether the bags are to be checked; use 'bags to check' or 'checked bags'.
Mispronouncing 'any' with a long vowel; it is 'EN-ee' in careful speech and 'nee' in fast speech.

conversation.text: "Do you have any bags to check?" "Just one suitcase."

senses.definition: A short entry of the proceedings of a court; the register containing them; the office containing the register.
senses.example: The clerk recorded the judge's brief ruling in the court docket before adjourning for lunch.

senses.definition: A schedule of cases awaiting action in a court.
An agenda of things to be done.
senses.example: My manager reviewed the docket for tomorrow's board meeting, checking each item before we arrived.

senses.definition: A ticket or label fixed to something, showing its contents or directions to its use.
senses.example: The shop attached a docket to the box stating the sender, weight, and handling instructions.

senses.definition: To enter or inscribe in a docket, or list of causes for trial.
senses.example: The court dockets all pending civil cases on the first Monday of each month for scheduling.

senses.definition: To label a parcel, etc.
senses.example: to docket goods

senses.definition: To make a brief abstract of (a writing) and endorse it on the back of the paper, or to endorse the title or contents on the back of; to summarize.
senses.example: to docket letters and papers

senses.definition: To make a brief abstract of and inscribe in a book.
senses.example: judgments regularly docketed

core.definition: A court's list of cases scheduled for hearing or trial, or the official record of court proceedings.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the second a short, reduced i, so it ends like kit. The first vowel is the cot vowel, not the oh vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It sounds businesslike and can suggest a busy schedule.
nuance.usage_note: In American courts, the docket is the schedule of cases, and lawyers say they have a case on the docket today. Americans also use docket loosely for a crowded agenda, as in a full docket for the meeting. Calendar is an alternative in many courts, but docket is standard in legal writing. As a verb, docket means to enter a case on the list.

distinctions.note: Calendar is a general word for a schedule; in court it can mean the same thing, but docket emphasizes a formal list of cases.
An agenda lists topics for a meeting, while a docket is a formal list of cases for a court, though Americans sometimes use it loosely for a crowded schedule.

examples.everyday: My lawyer friend said her docket is packed until Friday, so lunch will have to wait.
examples.professional: Please add the vendor contract to the docket for Thursday's leadership meeting.
examples.analytical: A crowded docket can delay justice, which is why courts sometimes set priorities for certain kinds of cases.

nuance.analogy: A court docket is like a restaurant reservation book: it lists who is scheduled and when.
common_mistakes: Confusing the verb with the noun: the clerk dockets the case means enters it on the list.
Using docket to mean a receipt or ticket; in American English it refers to a court list or agenda.

senses.definition: A dog, especially a small one.
senses.example: That's such a cute little doggy, Keira!

senses.definition: Synonym of corporal.
senses.example: The old doggy kept the new recruits marching at dawn, shouting every order without mercy.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of doggy style.
senses.example: Her favorite position is doggy.

senses.definition: Doggy style.
senses.example: The toddler crawled doggy across the rug, chasing the rolling ball.

senses.definition: Suggestive of or in the manner of a dog.
senses.example: He gave a doggy grin and wagged his shoulders when the boss walked in.

senses.definition: Fond of dogs.
senses.example: My aunt is a doggy person, so every holiday dinner includes a dog on her lap.

senses.definition: Doggy style.
senses.example: The toddler crawled doggy across the rug, chasing the rolling ball.

core.definition: An informal, affectionate name for a dog, especially a small or young one, often used when talking to a child or pet.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and end with a clear long ee sound, as in DAW-gee. Keep the middle g soft and voiced, and avoid turning it into a j sound.

nuance.connotation: Warm and affectionate when used for a pet, but childish when used by adults for a grown man or woman.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say doggy mainly in baby talk, with children, or to a friendly pet, as in 'Hi, doggy!' Adults usually say dog, or puppy for a young animal. Be careful with the phrase 'doggy style,' which is slang for a sexual position and should be avoided in polite company. The useful everyday phrase is 'doggy bag,' the container a restaurant gives you for taking home leftovers.

distinctions.note: Dog is the standard neutral word for the animal, while doggy is informal, cute, and usually used with small pets or children.
Puppy refers specifically to a young dog, whereas doggy can refer to any small dog regardless of age, with a warm tone.
Doggie and doggy are both informal and nearly interchangeable in American English, though doggie is slightly more common in writing.

examples.everyday: Hey, good doggy, do you want a belly rub?
examples.professional: Our pet-friendly office policy allows employees to bring a doggy bed to their desks, as long as the animal is well behaved.
examples.analytical: Calling the animal 'doggy' domesticates it into a small, harmless companion, which reveals how language turns a working animal into a family member.

nuance.analogy: Doggy is to dog as a cuddly nickname is to a full name: the same creature, said with more warmth.
nuance.etymology: From dog plus the diminutive suffix -y.
common_mistakes: Saying 'doggy style' in ordinary conversation; this is a sexual slang term, so avoid it outside of intimate or joking contexts.
Using doggy for an adult's dog in formal writing; use dog instead.

senses.definition: In a domestic manner.
At home, playing in one's home ground.
senses.example: The team played domestically for the first three weeks before traveling to face rivals.

core.definition: Within a country's own borders, or in a way that concerns the home or household.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MES, the second syllable. The final -ly is pronounced as a clear "lee" sound, and the middle syllables are weak.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes location or scope without emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use domestically most often in business, news, and policy contexts, such as domestically produced goods or domestically focused marketing. In casual speech they would usually say at home or in the US. It is a clear, professional word rather than a casual one.

distinctions.note: Nationally refers to a whole nation or national scope, while domestically emphasizes that something happens inside one country as opposed to abroad.
At home is the everyday phrase for being in one's house or country, while domestically is more formal and used for business or policy.

examples.everyday: The shirts are made domestically, so they usually cost more than the imported ones.
examples.professional: We're focusing our marketing domestically this year before expanding abroad.
examples.analytical: The policy was defined domestically, shaped by local interest groups rather than by international pressure.

nuance.analogy: Like a neighborhood bakery that sells only to its own town, domestically means the activity stays inside one place.
nuance.etymology: From domestic (adjective) plus the suffix -ally, meaning in a manner that relates to.
common_mistakes: Confusing domestically with domestically meaning at someone's house. In US business use it means within the country.
Stressing the first syllable instead of MES.

senses.definition: One who, or that which, dominates.
A node that dominates another.
senses.example: In the control-flow graph, the entry block is the dominator of every other block.

senses.definition: (uncommon) A male dominant.
senses.example: The silverback was the dominator of the troop, and the younger males kept their distance.
senses.label: uncommon

core.definition: A person or thing that dominates, meaning exercises control or power over others or dominates a position or market.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, DAH, as in 'dominate,' and the ending is -AY-ter with a clear American r. Learners often say 'dom-in-AH-tor' by analogy with 'emperor,' which is wrong.

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral; usually describes someone who controls others, but in technical contexts it is simply a precise term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this noun in everyday speech and would more often say 'bully,' 'control freak,' or 'domineering person.' In a meeting or conversation, 'dominant personality' is more natural. In computing and graph theory, it is a technical term with a specific meaning.

distinctions.note: Dominator is a rare noun for a person or node that actively dominates; dominant is more common as an adjective describing what prevails.
A bully targets weaker people through intimidation; a dominator can be a neutral or even benign force, such as a team or node that controls a position.

examples.everyday: Don't let him be the dominator in every game on the playground; let the other kids pick a turn too.
examples.professional: Our senior engineer is a dominator in design meetings, so junior ideas rarely get a fair hearing.
examples.analytical: Classic compiler theory defines a dominator as a node that must be passed through on every path to another node.

nuance.analogy: In a graph, a dominator is like the only tollbooth on the road into town: every traveler must pass through it.
nuance.etymology: From dominate, from Latin dominari, 'to rule,' with the agent suffix -or.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'DOH-mih-nay-ter' or with the first syllable stressed as 'DOH' rather than 'DAH'.
Using 'dominator' as a synonym for the adjective 'dominant,' as in 'the dominator team.'

senses.definition: Destiny, especially terrible.
An undesirable fate; an impending severe occurrence or danger that seems inevitable.
Dread; a feeling of danger, impending danger, darkness, or despair.
Death.
senses.example: They met an untimely doom when the mineshaft caved in.

senses.definition: The Last Judgment; or, an artistic representation thereof.
To pronounce judgment or sentence on; to condemn.
senses.example: a criminal doomed to death

senses.definition: To destine; to fix irrevocably the ill fate of.
To be extremely pessimistic about something.
Initialism of didn't organize, only moved; used in compounds designating a miscellaneous collection of items which one has failed to properly organize.
senses.example: I tried to organize my stuff but just ended up making a big doom pile.

core.definition: A terrible fate or ruin that seems certain to happen, or a feeling of dread about the future.

pronunciation.tip: One syllable with a long oo sound, like 'boom'. Do not reduce it to 'dum' with a short u. The final m is clear, so do not add a vowel after it.

nuance.connotation: Negative, suggesting disaster, ruin or hopelessness. It can be used humorously ('Doom and gloom').
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say 'doom and gloom' about pessimistic news or people, and 'doomed' to describe a plan that will fail ('The project is doomed'). In casual conversation it can be dramatic and playful. In religious or literary speech it describes God's judgment or final ruin.

distinctions.note: Fate is neutral and can be good or bad; doom always implies a bad, inescapable outcome.
Dread is the emotional feeling of fear; doom is the outcome that is feared, or the sense that disaster is coming.

examples.everyday: Don't listen to him; he always talks about doom and gloom.
examples.professional: The forecast looks like doom for the old product line unless we invest in the new platform.
examples.analytical: Many ancient prophets proclaimed doom on nations that had abandoned justice, and their warnings shaped later moral thought.

nuance.analogy: Doom is like a storm cloud that you can see building on the horizon, heavy and certain, even before the rain starts.
nuance.etymology: From Old English 'dōm', meaning judgment, decision or law, the same root as 'deem'.
common_mistakes: Using 'doom' as a neutral word for any fate, when it always means a bad outcome.
Pronouncing it with a short u like 'dum' or 'dumb'.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture, doom is often the judgment that falls on sinners or nations. The Hebrew word 'mishpat' means judgment or justice, and the Greek 'krima' means judgment or sentence. In Isaiah 13 the prophet describes the doom of Babylon. In Joel 2 the day of the Lord is described as a day of darkness and gloom.

doom.etymology: From Middle English *doom*, *dom*, from Old English *dōm* (“judgement”), from **dōm*, from Proto-Germanic **dōmaz*, from Proto-Indo-European **dʰóh₁mos*.

senses.definition: Decline in judgment and other cognitive functions, associated with aging; senility.
senses.example: His memory failed badly in his dotage, and he forgot his own grandchildren's names.

senses.definition: Fondness or attentiveness, especially to an excessive degree.
senses.example: Her dotage on her youngest son embarrassed the rest of the family at every gathering.

senses.definition: Foolish utterance(s); drivel.
senses.example: Stop spouting such dotage at the dinner table, Uncle Ray, and pass the potatoes.

core.definition: The stage of old age when a person's memory and judgment decline; senility, or a period of foolish fondness in old age.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, DOH. The final "-age" is reduced to "ij" and is not pronounced "ahj." The "t" is clear.

nuance.connotation: Negative or teasing. It can be rude when describing a real person, but it is common as a playful remark about oneself or a friend.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use "dotage" mostly in the phrase "in one's dotage," which can be said with humor or with real sympathy. Saying it directly to an elderly person would be rude, so use it when talking about someone who is not present or in a joking way with friends. Americans might say "getting senile" or "losing it" in casual speech.

distinctions.note: "Old age" is neutral and respectful, while "dotage" specifically suggests mental decline.
"Senility" is a clinical or serious term for mental decline, while "dotage" is more literary and can be teasing.

examples.everyday: My grandfather is in his dotage, but he still beats me at cards, so don't underestimate him.
examples.professional: Our founder seems to be in his dotage, so the board has started planning the succession.
examples.analytical: Critics often treated the poet's late work as the product of dotage, overlooking its deliberate formal experiments.

nuance.analogy: Dotage is like the last chapter of a long book, when the writing gets looser and the story loses its shape.
nuance.etymology: From dote, "to be foolish or weak-minded," with the noun suffix -age.
common_mistakes: Using "dotage" as a polite term about an elderly person in their presence.
Confusing it with "doting," which means showing excessive love.

dotage.etymology: From Middle English *dotage*, from *doten* (“to dote”) + *-age*; equivalent to *dote* + *age*.

senses.definition: A disadvantageous aspect of something that is normally advantageous.
senses.example: The downside of obtaining a higher rank is that far more work is expected.

senses.definition: A downward tendency, especially in the price of shares etc.
The side of something that is at the bottom, or that is intended to face downward.

core.definition: The disadvantage or negative part of something that is usually good, such as a plan, job, or product.

pronunciation.tip: Stress DOWN and make the second syllable a clear, long i sound. Do not reduce the final d to a schwa; it is a plain d sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It names a drawback without necessarily making it a deal-breaker.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use downside often in business meetings and everyday decisions, usually with the phrase 'the downside is' or 'the only downside'. It is informal enough for casual talk but also common in professional settings. A natural reply is 'Yeah, what's the trade-off?' or 'Okay, is it worth it?'

distinctions.note: Drawback is a standard, neutral word for a disadvantage; downside is a bit more informal and is used especially in business talk.
Disadvantage is more formal and often relates to a person's position in a comparison; downside refers to a feature of a choice.
Risk is the chance of a bad outcome in the future, while downside is a known negative aspect.

collocations: weigh the upside and the downside

examples.everyday: The apartment is cheap, but the downside is that it's far from work.
examples.professional: The downside of this proposal is that it requires two more months of testing.
examples.analytical: Every moral good has its downside, and an honest ethics must name the costs rather than hide them.

nuance.analogy: A downside is the other side of a coin: a good feature always has a reverse side.
nuance.etymology: From down plus side, meaning the lower or unfavorable side.
common_mistakes: Using downside as a verb, which is not standard.
Writing 'down side' as two words in formal writing.

conversation.text: The downside is that it will take longer to build.
Are there any downsides to switching vendors?
The only downside is the higher price.

senses.definition: To attract.
senses.example: Their concerts draw in big crowds.

senses.definition: To get (someone) involved.
senses.example: They drew in the quiet boy who hadn't wanted to participate.

senses.definition: To approach.
senses.example: They saw that the night was quickly drawing in, so they pitched their tent.

senses.definition: To become dark earlier as a result of seasonal change.
senses.example: It's that time of year again when the evenings really start to draw in.

senses.definition: To reduce or contract; to become shorter.
senses.example: In late autumn the evenings draw in early, so we turn on the porch lights by five.

core.definition: To attract people or things, or to get someone involved in an activity or situation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the particle IN in most American speech, with draw getting lighter secondary stress. In draw her in, the words run together: draw-er-IN.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive when attracting; negative when pressuring someone into something.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use draw in for customers or crowds: The new store draws in a lot of shoppers. It also means pulling someone into a conflict: Don't draw me in to your fight. The sense the days draw in, for shorter winter days, is mainly British; Americans say the days get shorter.

distinctions.note: Attract is a general word for pulling interest; draw in can suggest actively pulling someone into a place or situation.
Draw in brings someone into involvement; draw out encourages someone to speak or makes something last longer.

collocations: draw someone in to a scheme

examples.everyday: That bakery smell always draws me in, so I end up buying a muffin.
examples.professional: The new onboarding program should draw in more junior engineers who don't yet feel part of the team.
examples.analytical: The argument draws readers in by framing a familiar problem in an unfamiliar way.

nuance.analogy: It is like a gentle tide pulling a swimmer toward shore without anyone pushing.
common_mistakes: Putting a pronoun after draw in: say draw him in, not draw in him.
Using draw in for a car pulling into a space; Americans say pull in.

senses.definition: One who dreams.
Someone whose beliefs are far from realistic.
Any anglerfish of the family Oneirodidae.
A swallow-winged puffbird (Chelidoptera tenebrosa)

core.definition: A person who imagines or hopes for big goals that may seem unrealistic; also, someone who dreams while asleep.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, DREE, and the final -er is an unstressed r-colored schwa, not an 'air' sound. Keep the r at the end, so it sounds like 'DREE-mer' rather than 'DREE-mah'.

nuance.connotation: Mixed; it can be affectionate and hopeful, or a mild criticism that someone is impractical.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say he's a dreamer with a fond sigh or a teasing tone, meaning the person has big ideas but may lack a plan. In US politics, Dreamers, capitalized, refers to young undocumented immigrants brought to the country as children, and it is a common news term tied to the DREAM Act and DACA. A natural reply to he's a dreamer might be 'Well, somebody has to be.'

distinctions.note: An idealist holds principled ideals about how the world should be, while a dreamer may hope for things without a plan to achieve them.
A visionary is respected for foresight and practical ideas, while a dreamer may be seen as impractical.
A daydreamer drifts mentally while awake, while a dreamer may be a person with big hopes in general.

examples.everyday: Dad's always been a dreamer, planning a boat trip to Alaska that never quite happens.
examples.professional: She's a dreamer on the roadmap, but her prototypes always ship, so I'd take her ideas seriously.
examples.analytical: Rather than dismiss the dreamer, a good analysis asks which hopes are smuggled into the plan and which assumptions the dream quietly rests on.

nuance.analogy: A dreamer is like an architect who draws castles on napkins: the sketch matters only if someone turns it into a building.
nuance.etymology: From dream (Old English drēam) plus the agent suffix -er, meaning one who dreams.
common_mistakes: Confusing dreamer with Dreamers in US politics, which refers to a specific group of young immigrants.
Using dreamer only for someone asleep, when Americans mostly use it for an impractical hopeful person.
Pronouncing the final -er as a full 'air' sound instead of a reduced r-colored vowel.
nuance.biblical_note: In Genesis 37:19 Joseph's brothers mock him as this dreamer, referring to the dreams he has reported of sheaves and stars bowing down to him. The Hebrew verb behind dream here is chalam (ḥālam), to dream, and the brothers use the word with contempt, not admiration. In Jude 1:8, RSV uses dreamers for false teachers who defile the flesh and reject authority, where the Greek is enypniazomenoi, meaning those who dream or who are lost in visions, and the letter condemns them for their unreliable claims.

senses.definition: An instance of something drooping.
senses.example: The drooping of the tomato plants signaled that the soil needed water.

senses.definition: That droops or droop.
senses.example: drooping flowers

core.definition: Hanging down or bending downward, losing firmness, strength or energy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable with a long oo sound. The ing ending is short and unstressed, so say DROO-ping, not DROO-peeng.

nuance.connotation: Neutral when describing plants or objects; mildly negative when describing people or spirits.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use drooping to describe branches, flowers, eyelids or shoulders that hang or sag: 'a drooping willow.' It is common in everyday descriptions and in writing. It describes a current state, while droopy describes a lasting quality. It is neither formal nor rude.

distinctions.note: Drooping describes a current action or state, while droopy describes a more lasting quality, as in droopy eyelids.
Sagging suggests weight pulling something down, while drooping suggests loss of firmness or strength.

examples.everyday: The drooping branches of the willow almost touched the lake.
examples.professional: The drooping sales line on the chart prompted a review of our pricing.
examples.analytical: A drooping curve in the aggregate tells us little until we decompose it by cohort.

nuance.analogy: Like a plant on a hot porch: still standing, but bent under its own weight.
nuance.etymology: Middle English drupen, from Old English drūpian, meaning to droop.
common_mistakes: Using drooping for something that is simply tilted; it implies sagging or loss of firmness.
Saying DROOP-eeng with a long final vowel, rather than a short ing.

senses.definition: To deliver; to deposit or leave; to allow passengers to alight.
senses.example: Can you drop the kids off at school?

senses.definition: To fall asleep.
senses.example: After two glasses of whiskey, Tom soon dropped off in front of the television.

senses.definition: To fall off:
senses.example: The leaves were slowly dropping off the tree.

senses.definition: To drop from, fall from.
senses.example: The leaves were slowly dropping off the tree.

senses.definition: To drop, fall.
senses.example: The leaves hung on until the end of November, then dropped off quickly.

senses.definition: To abandon or give up on (something); to be abandoned or given up on.
senses.example: My lawyer said some of those charges will be dropped off.

senses.definition: To end a connection with a telephone queue, either by hanging up or after being served or processed.
senses.example: As soon as a caller drops off, we'll have an open line and maybe you can reach us then.

senses.definition: To lessen or reduce.
senses.example: Sales have dropped off in recent months.

senses.definition: (dated) To die.
senses.example: Poor old Ned finally dropped off last winter, peacefully in his sleep.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: To take someone or something to a place and leave them there.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on OFF. Many Americans pronounce off with the same vowel as cot, so ahf and awf are both acceptable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and practical; it describes a simple logistical action.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use drop off constantly for taking kids to school, leaving a package at a store, or dropping someone at the airport. The verb is separable: drop them off or drop off the kids. In informal speech it also means to fall asleep, as in I dropped off during the movie, and to decline, as in sales dropped off. Pick up is the common opposite.

distinctions.note: Drop off is about leaving something or someone at a place; drop by is about visiting briefly.
Pick up means collecting someone or something; drop off is the opposite action at the same place.

collocations: drop off the kids at school

examples.everyday: Can you drop me off at the grocery store on your way home?
examples.professional: I'll drop off the signed contract at the front desk before noon.
examples.analytical: The sociologist noted that the daily routine of dropping children off at school reflects a particular kind of neighborhood trust.

nuance.analogy: It is like leaving a parcel on someone's porch and driving away.
nuance.etymology: From drop, meaning to let fall or set down, plus off, meaning away from a place.
common_mistakes: Placing the pronoun after off; say drop me off, not drop off me.
Confusing drop off with drop by when you mean a quick visit.

conversation.text: Can you drop me off at the train station?
I dropped the kids off at school at eight.
Sales dropped off after the holidays.
I dropped off on the couch during the movie.
I'll drop you off at the entrance.
I need to drop off a package at the post office.
Sorry, I have to drop off for another meeting.

senses.definition: A heavy truck, for carrying loose, bulk cargo (e.g. soil, gravel, grain), having a hinged bed that allows the contents to be unloaded onto the ground via dumping.
senses.example: The construction crew loaded the dump truck with gravel before heading to the site.

senses.definition: A large pair of buttocks.
senses.example: My brothers teased me for years about my dump truck, which was not nice at all.

core.definition: A heavy truck with a tilting open box used to haul loose material such as dirt or gravel and unload it by tipping the bed.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on DUMP, with a weaker secondary stress on TRUCK in this compound. The r in 'truck' is American, so the tongue curls back, and the vowel is short.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a practical, everyday term for a work vehicle.
nuance.usage_note: Americans always say dump truck for this vehicle; British speakers say 'tipper lorry' or 'tipper'. The term is common in construction, road work and everyday talk, and people often shorten it to 'dump' when the context is clear. The slang sense, meaning a large pair of buttocks, is informal and can be rude, so avoid it in mixed company.

distinctions.note: Tipper is the British term for this vehicle; Americans say dump truck.
A tractor-trailer carries sealed freight over long distances, while a dump truck carries loose bulk material over short distances.

collocations: a dump truck full of gravel

examples.everyday: There's a dump truck blocking the driveway, so we'll have to park on the street.
examples.professional: The contractor booked two dump trucks to haul the excavated soil off the site by Thursday.
examples.analytical: Philosophers of technology sometimes take the dump truck as a plain example of a tool whose function is fully visible in its design.

nuance.analogy: A dump truck is like a wheelbarrow scaled up to a whole truck bed.
nuance.etymology: Compound of 'dump' (to tip out) and 'truck' (a heavy wheeled vehicle).
common_mistakes: Saying 'tipper truck' or 'tipper lorry' in the US; Americans say dump truck.
Using 'dump truck' for a garbage truck; a garbage truck is a garbage truck or trash truck.
Mispronouncing the compound with equal stress on both words; the first word is stronger.

senses.definition: Declining; growing less.
senses.example: There is dwindling support for New Labor.

senses.definition: A gradual reduction to nothing.
senses.example: The dwindling of our savings account worried us after the second layoff.

core.definition: Becoming steadily smaller in number, amount or strength over time.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle vowel is usually dropped, so the l becomes a syllable on its own; say DWIND-ling with the d and l running together.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a decline and often suggests concern or loss.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'dwindling' in news, business and everyday speech to describe shrinking supplies, numbers or interest, such as 'dwindling sales' or 'dwindling savings'. It is more descriptive than 'going down' and usually signals a gradual process. In casual talk, 'running low' or 'getting smaller' is a common alternative.

distinctions.note: Declining is a general word for becoming less, while dwindling suggests a slow shrinking that may approach nothing.
Shrinking often refers to physical size, while dwindling is used more for numbers, resources and support.
Decreasing is neutral and technical, while dwindling feels more descriptive and emotional.

examples.everyday: Our coffee supply is dwindling, so we should pick up more before the weekend.
examples.professional: The dwindling number of active users means we need to revisit our retention strategy this quarter.
examples.analytical: A dwindling congregation raises the question of whether institutional decline signals spiritual decline or only a change in form.

nuance.analogy: Like a candle burning lower and lower until only a small flame remains.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English dwinen 'to waste away', with the frequentative suffix -le, from Old English dwīnan.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle vowel as a separate syllable, such as DWIN-duh-ling.
Using 'dwindling' as a noun in ordinary speech; it is almost always an adjective.
Confusing 'dwindle' (verb) with 'dwindling' (adjective) in sentence structure.

senses.definition: In a dyspeptic manner.

core.definition: In a sour, irritable, or gloomy manner, as if suffering from indigestion.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on TIK, not on PEP. Pronounce the first syllable as 'dis' and the final -ly as 'lee'.

nuance.connotation: Negative, describing a grumpy or sour manner.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this adverb in conversation. It appears mainly in literary description of a grumpy character or in criticism. In everyday speech they would say grumpily, in a sour mood, or like he had a stomachache. Using it aloud can sound bookish or playful.

distinctions.note: Grumpily is the everyday word for acting irritable, while dyspeptically suggests irritability with a sour, stomach-related flavor and is more literary.
Sourly describes an unpleasant expression or tone, while dyspeptically describes a broader gloomy and irritated manner.

examples.professional: The manager responded dyspeptically to the budget request, so we waited until Monday to ask again.
examples.analytical: The critic wrote dyspeptically about the film's pacing, as though every scene had disagreed with him.

nuance.analogy: Speaking dyspeptically is like talking with a stomachache: every word comes out sour.
nuance.etymology: From dyspeptic, from Greek dyspeptos 'hard to digest', with the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable: the stress falls on TIK, not on PEP.
Using dyspeptically to describe a medical symptom; it describes a manner of speaking or behaving.

senses.definition: Lack of difficulty; the ability to do something easily.
senses.example: He played the ukelele with ease.

senses.definition: Comfort, a state or quality lacking unpleasantness, particularly:
senses.example: She enjoyed the ease of living in a house where the servants did all the work.

senses.definition: Freedom from effort; leisure, rest.
senses.example: We took our ease on the patio.

senses.definition: Freedom from financial effort or worry; affluence.
senses.example: His inheritance catapulted him into a life of ease.

senses.definition: Freedom from embarrassment or awkwardness; grace.
senses.example: She dealt with the faculty with combined authority and ease.

senses.definition: Relief, an end to discomfort, particularly:
senses.example: Take one pill every 12 hours to provide ease from pain.

senses.definition: Followed by of or from: release from or reduction of pain, hardship, or annoyance.
senses.example: Take one pill every 12 hours to provide ease from pain.

senses.definition: Release from constraint, obligation, or a constrained position.
senses.example: At ease, soldier!

senses.definition: Additional space provided to allow greater movement.
senses.example: Add some ease to the waist measurement.

senses.definition: To free (something) from pain, worry, agitation, etc.
senses.example: He eased his conscience by confessing.

senses.definition: To alleviate, assuage or lessen (pain).
To give respite to (someone).
senses.example: The provision of extra staff eased their workload.

senses.definition: To reduce the difficulty of (something).
senses.example: We had to ease the entry requirements.

senses.definition: To move (something) slowly and carefully.
senses.example: He eased the cork from the bottle.

senses.definition: To lessen in intensity.
senses.example: The pain eased overnight.

senses.definition: To proceed with little effort.
senses.example: The car eased onto the motorway.

senses.definition: To reduce speed.
To loosen or slacken the tension on a line.
senses.example: We eased the boom vang, then lowered the sail.

core.definition: Freedom from difficulty, effort or strain; a state of comfort, calm and relaxation.

pronunciation.tip: Use a long, tense ee vowel and end with a clear z sound, not an s. It is one syllable, so do not add a schwa at the end.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes comfort and smooth effort, and it is rarely used in a negative sense.
nuance.usage_note: Common in everyday American speech in phrases like at ease, with ease and ease of mind. Americans also use it as a verb, as in ease the pain. When someone says you can do something with ease, they mean it looks effortless to them.

distinctions.note: Ease is the noun for the state of not struggling; easy is the adjective describing a task or a relaxed person.
Comfort is physical or emotional well-being; ease focuses on the absence of difficulty or effort.
Facility means skill or a building; ease is the more natural everyday word for effortless doing.

examples.everyday: She put me at ease right away, so the job interview felt like a normal conversation.
examples.professional: The new dashboard offers real ease of use, so managers can filter the results without any training.
examples.analytical: Many philosophers separate the ease of a practiced skill from its correctness, since a habit can feel effortless and still be mistaken.

nuance.analogy: Like a well-worn path that lets you walk without thinking about each step.
nuance.etymology: From Old French aise, meaning comfort or ease, of uncertain origin.
common_mistakes: Using easy as a noun: say with ease or ease of use, not with easy.
Pronouncing the final sound as s instead of a voiced z.

senses.definition: Able to be eaten; edible.
Anything edible; food.
senses.example: We packed some eatables for the hike: sandwiches, fruit, and trail mix.

core.definition: Safe and fit to be eaten; able to be eaten, usually said of food.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, EE. The second syllable is a quick, reduced 'uh', so say EE-tuh-bul, not EE-tay-bul.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and practical; it addresses whether food is safe or acceptable to eat, not whether it tastes good.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use eatable mostly in casual speech, such as 'Is this still eatable?' or 'Nothing in the fridge was eatable.' In formal or written contexts, edible is the standard word. Eatable often implies just barely fit to eat, as in 'The soup was barely eatable.'

distinctions.note: Edible is the standard word in writing and on labels; eatable is more casual and often suggests merely acceptable.
Delicious praises taste, while eatable only says food can be eaten, so calling food eatable is weak praise.

examples.everyday: The leftover pizza is still eatable, so don't throw it out yet.
examples.professional: Quality control said the batch was eatable, but the texture was off, so we pulled it from the shelves.
examples.analytical: Something can be eatable in a narrow sense, safe to swallow, without being nourishing or good.

nuance.analogy: Eatable is the 'can I eat this?' word, like food that has passed only the first safety check.
nuance.etymology: From English 'eat' plus the suffix '-able', meaning able to be eaten.
common_mistakes: Saying eatable for food you find delicious; it means safe or acceptable, not tasty.
Pronouncing the second syllable as a full 'tay' instead of a reduced 'tuh'.

senses.definition: Initialism of expected date of confinement.
senses.example: Her EDC is March 14, so her manager is planning the handoff for early March.

senses.definition: Initialism of everyday carry.
Initialism of electronic data capture.
senses.example: Our clinical trial team uses EDC software to record patient results directly into the database.

senses.definition: Initialism of endocrine disruptor chemical.
senses.example: Researchers found the EDC in plastic bottles could interfere with hormone signaling in lab mice.

senses.definition: Initialism of ethylene dichloride and 1,2-dichloroethane.
senses.example: The factory stored EDC in steel drums before shipping it to plastics manufacturers.

senses.definition: To carry every day; to carry daily.
senses.example: Many people love EDCing a utility knife in addition to their multitool.

core.definition: Everyday carry: the items a person routinely carries each day, such as a phone, wallet, keys or a small knife.

pronunciation.tip: Say the three letters separately, with the strongest stress on the last letter, C, which is pronounced 'see'. Do not try to say it as one word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests practicality and preparedness, though it can sound hobbyist or tactical.
nuance.usage_note: You hear EDC mainly among outdoor enthusiasts, knife and gear collectors, and people who enjoy practical gadgets. In medical settings, Americans say 'due date' rather than the older expanded form. In casual talk, say 'What's in your EDC?' and expect a list of small items.

distinctions.note: An EDC is what you carry every day; a bug-out bag is a packed emergency bag for leaving home quickly.
In pregnancy, the expected date of confinement is usually just called the due date; EDC in that sense is mostly a medical abbreviation.

examples.everyday: My EDC is just a wallet, keys, a flashlight and a small pocketknife.
examples.professional: Our safety training covers what field staff should keep in their EDC kits during site visits.
examples.analytical: An EDC list reveals a person's assumptions about risk, since each item answers a specific daily need.

nuance.analogy: An EDC is like the things you always reach for in your pockets, a small toolkit you never leave home without.
nuance.etymology: Initialism of everyday carry.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing EDC as one word, like 'ed-see'; say the three letters separately.
Confusing EDC with expected date of confinement in ordinary conversation about hobbies or gear.

senses.definition: The state of being elaborate.
Something elaborate.
senses.example: The elaborateness of the wedding cake amazed everyone, with its sugar roses and tiered layers.

core.definition: The quality of being complicated, detailed or carefully worked out, often with more decoration or detail than is needed.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on LAB, and the -ate ending is a reduced schwa, sounding like 'it,' not 'ate.' Keep the middle syllables light and unstressed.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It can describe admirable craft, but it often suggests unnecessary complexity.
nuance.usage_note: Americans usually prefer words like complexity, detail or fancy in everyday talk. Elaborateness sounds formal and is most natural when describing a plan, design, ritual or set of decorations. It can be praise for careful craft or a mild criticism of overcomplication, depending on context.

distinctions.note: Complexity refers to the number and interaction of parts, while elaborateness suggests added decoration or detail on top of what is necessary.
Intricacy describes fine, interlocking detail that is hard to follow, while elaborateness can also describe showy or excessive embellishment.

examples.everyday: My sister loves the elaborateness of her wedding cake, with five tiers and sugar roses.
examples.professional: The client asked us to cut the elaborateness of the dashboard, since most users only check three metrics.
examples.analytical: The elaborateness of the argument obscures its central claim, so the reader must work to find what the author is actually asserting.

nuance.analogy: A five-tier wedding cake with sugar flowers: its elaborateness is in the layers and decorations added beyond what the cake needs.
nuance.etymology: From elaborate, from Latin elaboratus 'worked out,' from elaborare 'to work out,' from ex- and laborare 'to work'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final syllables as /eɪt/ like the verb elaborate.
Using elaborateness when the simpler word 'detail' or 'complexity' fits better in everyday speech.

senses.definition: Pertaining to the reign of Queen Elizabeth I, monarch of England and Ireland, from 1558 to 1603.
Often preceded by new or second: pertaining to the reign of Queen Elizabeth II, monarch of the United Kingdom, from 1952 to 2022.
senses.example: Many commentators hoped the new Elizabethan age would bring fresh optimism to Britain.

senses.definition: Pertaining to the reign of Empress Elizabeth of Russia, from 1741 to 1762.
senses.example: The Elizabethan court in St. Petersburg was famous for its lavish balls and extravagant architecture.

senses.definition: A person (especially a writer) who lived during the reign of Queen Elizabeth I, monarch of England and Ireland, from 1558 to 1603.
senses.example: Marlowe is considered one of the great Elizabethans, though he died young in a tavern brawl.

senses.definition: A person who lived during the reign of Queen Elizabeth II, monarch of the United Kingdom, from 1952 to 2022.
senses.example: My grandmother, a proud Elizabethan, remembers the coronation on a borrowed black-and-white television.

core.definition: Relating to the reign of Queen Elizabeth I of England (1558 to 1603), or to the literature, drama and culture of that period.
